leads.caseName: Rh Kids, LLC v. Nationstar Mortgage, LLC
leads.text:
IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF THE STATE OF NEVADA 

RH KIDS, LLC, A CALIFORNIA 
LIMITED LIABILITY CORPORATION, 
Appellant, 
vs. 
NATIONSTAR MORTGAGE LLC D/B/A 
MR. COOPER, A DELAWARE LIMITED 
LIABILITY COMPANY, 
Respondent. 

No. 91058-COA 
ORDER OF AFFIRMANCE 

 RH Kids, LLC, appeals from a district court order of dismissal in 
an action to quiet title. Eighth Judicial District Court, Clark County; Hon. 
Jessica K. Peterson, Judge. 
 RH Kids was the owner of a residential property and initiated an 
action to quiet title. In the operative complaint, RH Kids raised several claims 
involving respondent Nationstar Mortgage LLC, the beneficiary of a deed of 
trust encumbering the property. As relevant to this matter, RH Kids alleged 
that the deed of trust had been extinguished as a matter of law under NRS 
106.240, which it alleged was triggered by a notice of intent to accelerate the 
underlying debt in a letter sent to the original borrowers more than ten years 
ago. 
 Nationstar later filed a motion to dismiss, asserting the facts as 
alleged were insufficient to state a claim for which relief could be granted. RH 
Kids opposed the motion. The district court ultimately issued a written order 
dismissing RH Kids’ NRS 106.240 claim. This appeal followed. 
 On appeal, RH Kids argues the district court erred by dismissing 
its NRS 106.240 claim. RH Kids argues that the court was required to take its 
 2 
allegations as true when it reviewed the motion to dismiss and that it 
erroneously found that the loan had not been accelerated when it evaluated 
the motion to dismiss. RH Kids contends that the terms of the deed of trust 
permitted acceleration of the loan and notes the complaint alleged the lender 
sent the original borrowers a notice more than ten years ago indicating its 
intent to accelerate the loan secured by the deed of trust. RH Kids further 
argues, because the loan was accelerated more than ten years ago, the deed of 
trust that secured that debt was extinguished pursuant to NRS 106.240. 
 We rigorously review a district court order granting an NRCP 
12(b)(5) motion to dismiss, accepting all of the plaintiff’s factual allegations as 
true and drawing every reasonable inference in the plaintiff’s favor to 
determine whether the allegations are sufficient to state a claim for relief. 
Buzz Stew, LLC v. City of N. Las Vegas, 124 Nev. 224, 227-28, 181 P.3d 670, 
672 (2008). A complaint should be dismissed for failure to state a claim “only 
if it appears beyond a doubt that [the plaintiff] could prove no set of facts, 
which, if true, would entitle [the plaintiff] to relief.” Id. at 228, 181 P.3d at 
672. 
 Having considered the parties’ arguments and the record before 
this court, we conclude the district court did not err by dismissing RH Kids’ 
NRS 106.240 claim. RH Kids’ arguments are contrary to several decisions 
issued by the Nevada Supreme Court. See LV Debt Collect, LLC v. Bank of 
N.Y. Mellon, 139 Nev. 232, 236 -37, 534 P.3d 693, 698 (2023) (explaining that 
recording a notice of default to institute nonjudicial foreclosure proceedings 
does not trigger NRS 106.240’s 10-year time frame in part because of the 
statutory cure period); ARNS Fund, LLC v. JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., No. 
88661, 2025 WL 3251312, at *1 (Nev. Nov. 20, 2025) (Order Affirming in Part, 
Reversing in Part and Remanding) (stating that “ merely defaulting on a loan 
 3 
or sending a letter informing the homeowner of their default [was] insufficient 
to trigger NRS 106.240” and rejecting an argument that the terms of the deed 
of trust rendered the debt wholly due when the borrower had the opportunity 
to cure the default). 
 As a result, we conclude that the ten-year period under NRS 
106.240 was not triggered by any events identified by RH Kids. In addition, to 
the extent that RH Kids argues that the district court was required to consider 
its contentions that NRS 106.240 was triggered as true, those statements were 
not factual allegations but rather constituted a legal conclusion, and legal 
conclusions need not be accepted as true by the court when reviewing a motion 
to dismiss pursuant to NRCP 12(b)(5). See Nev. Yellow Cab Corp. v. State, No. 
83014, 2022 WL 17367603, at *2 (Nev. Dec. 1, 2022) (Order of Affirmance) 
(explaining that allegations that are legal conclusions need not be accepted as 
true for purposes of NRCP 12(b)(5)). Accordingly, RH Kids fails to demonstrate 
the district court erred by dismissing this matter, and we 
 ORDER the judgment of the district court AFFIRMED.
1 

Bulla, C.J. 

Gibbons, J. Westbrook, J. 

1Insofar as RH Kids raises arguments that are not specifically addressed 
in this order, we conclude that they either do not present a basis for relief or 
need not be addressed. In addition, this court takes no action regarding the 
notice filed by Nationstar informing this court of the death of opposing counsel. 

 4 

cc: Hon. Jessica K. Peterson, District Judge 
Hong & Hong 
Troutman Pepper Hamilton Sanders LLP/Las Vegas 
RH Kids, LLC 
Eighth District Court Clerk

leads.caseName: Fidelity Bank Versus Stuart G. Coleman and Jerry Lathan
leads.text:
Fifth Circuit Court of Appeal 
State of Louisiana 

No. 26-C-548 

FIDELITY BANK 

versus 

STUART G. COLEMAN AND JERRY LATHAN 

IN RE STUART G. COLEMAN 
APPLYING FOR SUPERVISORY WRIT FROM THE TWENTY -FOURTH JUDICIAL DISTRICT 
COURT, PARISH OF JEFFERSON, STATE OF LOUISIANA, DIRECTED TO THE HONORABLE 
FRANK BRINDISI, DIVISION "E", No. 876-033 

Panel composed of Judges Susan M. Chehardy, 
John J. Molaison, Jr., and Scott U. Schlegel 

WRIT DENIED 

Relator, Stuart G. Coleman, seeks review of the trial court’s October 14, 
2026 judgment denying his declinatory exception of improper venue and his 
alternative motion to transfer. For the following reasons, we deny the writ 
application. 
Procedural History 

On May 20, 2026, Fidelity Bank sued relator and Jerry Lathan in the 24th 
Judicial District Court. Fidelity alleges that relator and Lathan are solidarily liable 
under their guaranties of a loan to Carillon Oaks Lincoln, LLC, an Alabama 
limited liability company. The petition grounded venue solely in La. C.C.P. art. 
42, alleging that relator is domiciled in Jefferson Parish. On May 27, 2026, 

November 18, 2026 

Fidelity amended its petition to correct Lathan’s surname and repeated the same 
venue allegation. Lathan answered and filed a reconventional demand without 
excepting to venue. 
Relator filed a declinatory exception of improper venue and, alternatively, a 
motion to transfer the action to Orleans Parish. In opposition, Fidelity relied on 
La. C.C.P. art. 77. 
The trial court heard the exception on September 29, 2026. Relator testified, 
and the court admitted Fidelity Exhibits 1 through 7 without objection but 
excluded Fidelity’s proposed Exhibit 8, an affidavit. The court denied the 
exception at the close of the hearing and signed a written judgment on October 14, 
2026. 
The clerk mailed notice of judgment on October 15, 2026, and relator filed 
his notice of intent the same day. The trial court set a return date of November 13, 
2026, and stayed proceedings on the merits pending this Court’s disposition. 
Relator timely filed this application on November 13, 2026. 
Assignment of Error 

Relator assigns a single error: 

The district court erred in denying Mr. Coleman’s exception of 
improper venue by treating the Conlin Street address’s use for 
receiving mail and suitability for service as substitutes for the 
supervision required by La. C.C.P. art. 77. Neither establishes that an 
office at that address had supervision over the loan and guaranty at 
issue. To the extent the district court implicitly found that such 
supervision existed, that finding is manifestly erroneous because it 
lacks a reasonable factual basis and is clearly wrong in light of the 
record as a whole. 

Relator asks this Court to reverse the judgment, sustain the exception, and 
remand with instructions to transfer the action to the Civil District Court for the 
Parish of Orleans. Alternatively, he asks this Court to vacate the judgment and 
remand the matter for the trial court to apply Article 77’s supervision requirement. 
Standard of Review 

Venue is a question of law, which this Court reviews de novo. Seghers v. 
LaPlace Equip. Co., 13-350 (La. App. 5 Cir. 2/12/14), 136 So.3d 64, 69. On the 
trial of a declinatory exception, a party may introduce evidence to support or 
controvert the objection when its grounds do not appear from the petition, the 
citation, or the return. La. C.C.P. art. 930. When the court admits evidence at that 
hearing, it must decide the exception on the evidence presented rather than on the 
allegations of the petition. Galata Chemicals, LLC v. Chromalox, Inc., 25-18 (La. 
App. 5 Cir. 7/2/25), 421 So.3d 971, 976, writ denied, 25-983 (La. 11/25/25), 421 
So.3d 533. 
Where a party introduces evidence at the hearing, “a manifest-error/clearly-
wrong standard accompanies the appellate court’s de novo review of the legal 
question of venue as to any underlying factual findings.” FBP Covington, LLC v. 
Fat Boy’s Pizza Franchise, LLC, No. 26-C-446, 2026 WL 3082800, at *2 (La. 
App. 5 Cir. Oct. 15, 2026). An appellate court may reverse a factual finding only 
if it finds that no reasonable factual basis exists for the finding and that the record 
establishes the finding is clearly wrong. Stobart v. State, Through Dep’t of Transp. 
& Dev., 617 So.2d 880, 882 (La. 1993). Relator does not dispute this framework. 
Relator contends, however, that the trial court’s oral remark reflects a legal 
error that interdicted the fact-finding process and therefore requires de novo 
review. He relies on Evans v. Lungrin, 97-0541 (La. 2/6/98), 708 So.2d 731, 735, 
in which the supreme court held that when one or more legal errors interdict the 
fact-finding process, the manifest-error standard no longer applies and, if the 
record is otherwise complete, the appellate court should conduct its own de novo 
review. 
The asserted error appears only in the trial court’s oral reasons. At the close 
of the hearing, the court stated its belief that the testimony and documents showed 

that the Conlin Street address “was the proper place for him to be served.” 
Appellate courts review judgments, not reasons for judgment, and a trial court’s 
oral or written reasons form no part of the judgment. Hosp. Serv. Dist. No. 1 of 
Par. of St. James v. Hosp. Serv. Dist. No. 3 of Par. of Lafourche, 25-202 (La. App. 
5 Cir. 11/26/25), 427 So.3d 297, 303, writs denied, 25-1634 (La. 3/25/26), 428 
So.3d 268; 25-1636 (La. 3/25/26), 428 So.3d 269. The supreme court has applied 
the same rule in declining to base the standard of review on a trial court’s reasons 
rather than on its judgment. Wooley v. Lucksinger, 09-0571 (La. 4/1/11), 61 So.3d 
507, 572. 
The trial court denied the exception after considering relator’s testimony, the 
exhibits admitted into evidence, and the parties’ briefing and argument. At the 
hearing, both parties identified supervision as the only disputed element of Article 
77. The judgment therefore rests on an implicit finding that the Conlin Street 
office had supervision over the matter sued upon. Relator acknowledges that, if 
the judgment is so read, the finding must be assessed under the manifest-error 
standard, and that the brevity of the oral reasons alone does not warrant de novo 
factfinding. Accordingly, we review that finding for manifest error. 
Burden of Proof 

This Court has held that when the grounds for an objection of improper 
venue do not appear on the face of the petition, the defendant bears the burden of 
offering evidence in support of his position. Seghers, 136 So.3d at 69; Galata 
Chemicals, 421 So.3d at 976. Other courts have stated that the party invoking a 
supplementary venue article must establish that it applies. See Johnson v. 
Acadiana Ry. Co., 96-263 (La. App. 3 Cir. 4/16/97), 693 So.2d 226, 230. 
Relator suggests that Fidelity bore the burden because it first raised Article 
77 in its opposition. We need not resolve that question. Fidelity introduced 
documentary evidence and elicited relator’s admissions on cross-examination, and 

that evidence furnishes a reasonable factual basis for the finding under either 
allocation. 

The Evidence 

Article 77 provides: 

An action against a person having a business office or 
establishment in a parish other than that where he may be sued under 
Article 42 only, on a matter over which this office or establishment 
had supervision, may be brought in the parish where this office or 
establishment is located. 

Relator conceded at the hearing, and concedes in his application, that the first 
requirement of Article 77 is satisfied: he has a business office or establishment at 
4425 Conlin Street in Jefferson Parish. He also concedes that Article 77 does not 
require exclusive supervision, personal ownership of an office, or a particular form 
of proof. The only question is whether the record furnishes a reasonable basis for 
the finding that the Conlin Street office supervised the loan and guaranty. 
Relator was the only witness, and he offered no exhibits.1 On direct 
examination, he testified that his home is on General Haig Street in New Orleans, 
where he lived when suit was filed. He pays property taxes in Orleans Parish and 
ordinarily works from a home office there. He described the Conlin Street address, 
his brother’s dermatology clinic, as a mail-drop arrangement at which clinic staff 
receive his mail. He stated that he performs no work there and has not maintained 
an office there for about seven years. He testified that he negotiated the loan and 
the later agreements in Orleans Parish or at his attorney’s downtown office, that he 
reviewed communications and made decisions in New Orleans, and that he signed 
the documents at his home office or at his attorney’s office. He also testified that 

1 Relator’s affidavit was attached to his exception but was never offered into evidence. “Evidence not properly and 
officially offered and introduced cannot be considered, even if it is physically placed in the record.” Denoux v. 
Vessel Mgmt. Servs., Inc., 07-2143 (La. 5/21/08), 983 So.2d 84, 88. Accordingly, we do not consider the affidavit, 
although it appears in the writ application. See State v. Nguyen, 25-312 (La. App. 5 Cir. 11/12/25), 427 So.3d 267, 
282, writ denied, 25-1475 (La. 5/12/26), 430 So.3d 1087, petition for cert. filed (U.S. July 6, 2026) (No. 26-19). 

neither his brother nor the clinic staff had any role in the loan, and that neither he 
nor the Conlin Street address supervised or administered the loan in Jefferson 
Parish. 
On cross-examination, relator acknowledged that the Conlin Street address 
appears in his guarantor signature block and in the notice provision of the 2022 
Loan Agreement. He acknowledged that the 2025 Loan Forbearance and 
Modification Agreement and its First Amendment identify him in their opening 
recitals as “a resident of the State of Louisiana … having an address of 4425 
Conlin Street, Metairie” and list that address for notices. He admitted that he 
signed the forbearance agreement under oath while represented by counsel. Asked 
whether he ever used his home address in the loan transaction, he answered, “For 
notices, no.” Asked whether he used it for anything, he answered that his home 
was where he did his business daily. 
Relator further acknowledged that he used his SGC Group email for this 
loan transaction. On September 9, 2026, twenty days before the hearing, he wrote 
to Fidelity requesting the loan’s 2025 principal and interest activity and its year-
end statement, and he signed that email “SGC Group, L.L.C. 4425 Conlin St 
Metairie, LA 70006.” He agreed that SGC Group, the management company he 
owns, is domiciled at 4425 Conlin Street, and that he is its registered agent and 
manager at that address. His Louisiana State Bar Association listing likewise gives 
Conlin Street as his address, although the listing notes that the parish shown is 
based on the member’s mailing address. The Secretary of State’s record for 
Carillon Oaks Lincoln Master Tenant, LLC shows that entity’s domicile at Conlin 
Street, with Lathan & Coleman LLC as its manager at the same address. Relator 
testified, however, that the Master Tenant was not involved in this loan. 
Fidelity called no witnesses. The trial court excluded the proposed affidavit 
of Fidelity’s executive vice president on relator’s hearsay objection. 

Law and Analysis 

Article 77 requires more than an office in the parish. “The office or 
establishment providing supervision over the matter in dispute must be located in 
that parish.” Johnson, 693 So.2d at 230. Where the record is silent on the 
essential element of supervision, Article 77 does not apply. Surridge v. Benanti, 
261 La. 282, 259 So.2d 324, 328 (1972). Whether the office had supervision over 
the matter is a question of fact. See Recile v. Weigel, 188 So.2d 636, 638 (La. App. 
4 Cir. 1966).

leads.caseName: Bank of N.Y. Mellon v. Estate of Beaudouin
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
Bank of N.Y. Mellon v Estate of Beaudouin 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06796 
 November 18, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Bank of New York Mellon, etc., appellant, 
 v 
 Estate of Jean Marie Beaudouin, etc., et al., defendants, Jerry Beaudouin, etc., et al., respondents. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on November 18, 2026 
 2024-10462, (Index No. 5794/13) 
 Mark C. Dillon, J.P. 
 Helen Voutsinas 
 Laurence L. Love 
 Elena Goldberg Velazquez, JJ. 

 Hinshaw & Culbertson LLP, New York, NY (Alexandra A. Kaminski and Charles W. Miller III of counsel), for appellant. 
 Anderson Bouman Wallshein PLLC, Melville, NY (Charles Wallshein of counsel), for respondents. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action to foreclose a mortgage, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Nassau County (Catherine Rizzo, J.), entered July 5, 2024. The order, insofar as appealed from, denied those branches of the plaintiff's motion which were pursuant to CPLR 306-b for leave to extend its time to serve the summons and complaint upon the defendants Andrelia Jerline Beaudouin, Henriette Carmelle Beaudouin, and Brianna Wilda Beaudouin and granted those branches of the cross-motion of the defendants Jerry Beaudouin, Andrelia Jerline Beaudouin, Henriette Carmelle Beaudouin, and Brianna Wilda Beaudouin which were pursuant to CPLR 5015(a)(4) to vacate an order of reference of the same court dated November 1, 2022, in effect, pursuant to CPLR 3211(a)(8) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendants Andrelia Jerline Beaudouin, Henriette Carmelle Beaudouin, and Brianna Wilda Beaudouin, and pursuant to CPLR 3215(c) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendant Jerry Beaudouin. 
 ORDERED that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs. 
 In September 2004, Jean Marie Beaudouin (hereinafter the decedent) executed a loan agreement and note secured by a mortgage on certain residential property located in Valley Stream. The decedent died intestate on February 22, 2010, survived by her husband, the defendant Jerry Beaudouin (hereinafter Jerry), and their daughters, then infants, the defendants Andrelia Jerline Beaudouin, Henriette Carmelle Beaudouin, and Brianna Wilda Beaudouin (hereinafter collectively the infant defendants). 
 On May 13, 2013, the plaintiff commenced this action to foreclose the mortgage against, among others, Jerry and the infant defendants (hereinafter collectively the defendants). In affidavits of service, a process server averred that on May 18, 2013, he served the infant defendants by delivering the summons and complaint to a person of suitable age and discretion at the infant defendants' dwelling place and mailed those documents to that address on May 28, 2013. In an order dated May 13, 2015, the Supreme Court, among other things, granted those branches of the plaintiff's ex parte motion which were for alternative service and to appoint a guardian ad litem [*2] (hereinafter GAL) for the infant defendants. Thereafter, the plaintiff purported to effectuate service by publication. 
 In an order dated November 1, 2022, the Supreme Court granted the plaintiff's motion, inter alia, for leave to enter a default judgment against the defendants and for an order of reference (hereinafter the November 2022 order). In December 2023, the plaintiff moved, among other things, pursuant to CPLR 306-b to extend the time to serve the summons and complaint upon the infant defendants. The defendants opposed the motion and cross-moved, inter alia, pursuant to CPLR 5015(a)(4) to vacate the November 2022 order, in effect, pursuant to CPLR 3211(a)(8) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against the infant defendants, and pursuant to CPLR 3215(c) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against Jerry. In an order entered July 5, 2024, the Supreme Court, among other things, denied those branches of the plaintiff's motion and granted those branches of the defendants' cross-motion. The plaintiff appeals. 
 Generally, service of a summons and complaint must be made within 120 days after the commencement of the action ( id. § 306-b). "If service is not made upon a defendant within the time provided in [CPLR 306-b], the court, upon motion, shall dismiss the action without prejudice as to that defendant, or upon good cause shown or in the interest of justice, extend the time for service" ( id. ). "Good cause and interest of justice are two separate and independent statutory standards" ( U.S. Bank N.A. v Bindra , 217 AD3d 719, 720 [internal quotation marks omitted]; see Leader v Maroney, Ponzini & Spencer , 97 NY2d 95, 104; Bumpus v New York City Tr. Auth. , 66 AD3d 26, 31). 
 "To establish good cause, a plaintiff must demonstrate reasonable diligence in attempting service" ( US Bank N.A. v Fink , 206 AD3d 858, 860; see Leader v Maroney, Ponzini & Spencer , 97 NY2d at 105-106). "The more flexible interest of justice standard accommodates late service that might be due to mistake, confusion, or oversight, so long as there is no prejudice to the defendant" ( U.S. Bank N.A. v Bindra , 217 AD3d at 720; see HSBC Bank USA, N.A. v Labin , 232 AD3d 861, 863). "The interest of justice standard requires a court to carefully analyze the factual setting of the case and to balance the competing interests presented by the parties" ( PNC Bank, N.A. v Sarfaty , 225 AD3d 721, 722; see Leader v Maroney, Ponzini & Spencer , 97 NY2d at 105). "Unlike an extension request premised on good cause, a plaintiff need not establish reasonably diligent efforts at service as a threshold matter" ( Leader v Maroney, Ponzini & Spencer , 97 NY2d at 105). "However, the court may consider diligence, or lack thereof, along with any other relevant factor in making its determination, including expiration of the Statute of Limitations, the meritorious nature of the cause of action, the length of delay in service, the promptness of a plaintiff's request for the extension of time, and prejudice to defendant" ( id . at 105-106; see PNC Bank, N.A. v Sarfaty , 225 AD3d at 722). "No one factor is determinative" ( HSBC Bank USA, N.A. v Labin , 232 AD3d at 864 [internal quotation marks omitted]). The determination of whether to grant the extension in the interest of justice is within the discretion of the motion court ( see U.S. Bank N.A. v Bindra , 217 AD3d at 720). 
 Here, the plaintiff failed to demonstrate reasonable diligence in serving the infant defendants, as the summons and complaint identified the infant defendants as in the care of a guardian ad litem and failed to offer a reasonable excuse for its more than ten-year delay in moving for an extension of time to effectuate service ( see OneWest Bank N.A. v All the Heirs at Law [Moran] , 240 AD3d 803, 806; HSBC Bank USA, N.A. v Labin , 232 AD3d at 863). The plaintiff also failed to establish that an extension of time to serve the summons and complaint upon the infant defendants was warranted in the interest of justice. Although the expiration of the statute of limitations would normally weigh in the plaintiff's favor, the record demonstrated that the delay in this action was attributable to the plaintiff's lack of diligence ( see OneWest Bank N.A. v All the Heirs at Law [Moran] , 240 AD3d at 806 ; US Bank N.A. v Fink , 206 AD3d at 861). Further, the plaintiff failed to rebut the inference of substantial prejudice that arose due to the protracted delay, as it failed to provide any evidence that the infant defendants had actual notice of the action within the 120-day service period ( see OneWest Bank N.A. v All the Heirs at Law [Moran] , 240 AD3d at 806 ; US Bank N.A. v Fink , 206 AD3d at 861). Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly denied those branches of the plaintiff's motion which were pursuant to CPLR 306-b for leave to extend its time to serve the [*3] summons and complaint upon the infant defendants. 
 Pursuant to CPLR 5015(a)(4), "[t]he court which rendered a judgment or order may relieve a party from it upon such terms as may be just, on motion of any interested person . . . upon the ground of . . . lack of jurisdiction to render the judgment or order." CPLR 309, which governs personal service upon an infant, incompetent, or conservatee, provides that "[p]ersonal service upon an infant shall be made by personally serving the summons within the state upon a parent or any guardian or any person having legal custody." 
 Here, although Jerry was served individually, he was not served in his capacity as the natural guardian of the infant defendants ( see US Bank N.A. v McGown , 200 AD3d 826, 828; cf. Fox v 18-05 215th St. Owners , 143 AD2d 804, 805). Because service of the summons and complaint did not comply with CPLR 309, the action was jurisdictionally defective insofar as asserted against the infant defendants ( see US Bank N.A. v McGown , 200 AD3d at 828; Kolodzinski v Ferreiras , 168 AD2d 431, 432). Accordingly, the infant defendants were entitled to vacatur of the November 2022 order and dismissal of the complaint pursuant to CPLR 3211(a)(8) insofar as asserted against them ( see US Bank N.A. v McGown , 200 AD3d at 828). 
 Further, dismissal of the complaint insofar as asserted against Jerry was warranted pursuant to CPLR 3215(c). The plaintiff failed to take proceedings for the entry of a default judgment within one year of Jerry's default and its excuses were conclusory and legally insufficient ( see US Bank Trust N.A. v Meyer , 244 AD3d 900, 902; Stark v Calvert Wright Architecture, P.C. , 216 AD3d 1028, 1029). Since the plaintiff failed to proffer a reasonable excuse for its delay, this Court need not determine whether the plaintiff had a potentially meritorious cause of action against Jerry ( see Doe v Garfinkel , 234 AD3d 929, 931; Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Brathwaite , 197 AD3d 557, 558). 
 The plaintiff's remaining contentions are without merit. 
 DILLON, J.P., VOUTSINAS, LOVE and GOLDBERG VELAZQUEZ, JJ., concur. 
 ENTER: 
 Darrell M. Joseph 
 Clerk of the Court

leads.caseName: Bank of N.Y. Mellon v. Willis
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
Bank of N.Y. Mellon v Willis 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06797 
 November 18, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Bank of New York Mellon, etc., respondent, 
 v 
 Hopeton Willis, etc., et al., appellants, et al., defendants. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on November 18, 2026 
 2025-15501, (Index No. 59705/23) 
 Francesca E. Connolly, J.P. 
 Valerie Brathwaite Nelson 
 Laurence L. Love 
 James P. McCormack, JJ. 

 Biolsi Law Group, P.C., New York, NY (Steven Alexander Biolsi and Joseph A. Jacobson of counsel), for appellants. 
 Pincus & Tarab, Attorneys at Law, PLLC, Uniondale, NY (Robert Markel of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action to foreclose a mortgage, the defendants Hopeton Willis and Sharon Willis appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Westchester County (David S. Zuckerman, J.), dated November 6, 2025. The order, insofar as appealed from, denied the motion of those defendants pursuant to CPLR 5015(a)(4) to vacate an order and judgment of foreclosure and sale (one paper) of the same court dated June 11, 2025. 
 ORDERED that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs. 
 In 2023, the plaintiff commenced this action against, among others, the defendants Hopeton Willis and Sharon Willis (hereinafter together the defendants) to foreclose a mortgage on certain real property located in Mount Vernon. The defendants interposed an answer to the complaint. In September 2024, the Supreme Court, inter alia, granted that branch of the plaintiff's unopposed motion which was for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendants. Thereafter, the plaintiff moved to confirm a referee's report and for a judgment of foreclosure and sale. The notice of motion indicated that it was returnable on June 18, 2025, and that opposition papers were due at least seven days before the return date ( see CPLR 2214[b]). In an order and judgment of foreclosure and sale dated June 11, 2025, the court granted the plaintiff's unopposed motion. 
 The defendants moved pursuant to CPLR 5015(a)(4) to vacate the order and judgment of foreclosure and sale. The defendants contended that the Supreme Court lacked jurisdiction to issue the order and judgment of foreclosure and sale because it was issued prior to the return date of the plaintiff's motion to confirm the referee's report and for a judgment of foreclosure and sale and before the defendants' time to submit opposition had expired, which they asserted was at 11:59 p.m. on June 11, 2025, several hours after the court issued the order and judgment of foreclosure and sale. Notably, in their motion to vacate the order and judgment of foreclosure and sale, the defendants did not seek an extension of the time to oppose the plaintiff's motion or assert that they had been prepared to timely oppose the plaintiff's motion. Rather, the defendants took the position that, since their motion was pursuant to CPLR 5015(a)(4), and not CPLR 5015(a)(1), they were not [*2] obligated to demonstrate a meritorious defense to the plaintiff's motion. Thus, the defendants did not address the merits of the plaintiff's motion to confirm the referee's report and for a judgment of foreclosure and sale or move to vacate the order and judgment of foreclosure and sale on any other ground. In an order dated November 6, 2025, the court, among other things, denied the defendants' motion. The defendants appeal. 
 Pursuant to CPLR 5015(a)(4), "[t]he court which rendered a judgment or order may relieve a party from it upon such terms as may be just, on motion of any interested person . . . upon the ground of . . . lack of jurisdiction to render the judgment or order." CPLR 5015(a)(4) "is designed to preserve objections so fundamental to the power of adjudication of a court that they survive even a final judgment or order" ( Lacks v Lacks , 41 NY2d 71, 74-75). The scope of CPLR 5015(a)(4) includes lack of subject matter jurisdiction, lack of personal jurisdiction, and improper service of a motion ( see Nozdrovicky v Multiviz Health Servs., Inc. , 240 AD3d 801, 802; Blue Lagoon, LLC v Reisman , 214 AD3d 938, 940). Here, the defendants do not deny proper service of the plaintiff's motion to confirm the referee's report and for a judgment of foreclosure and sale. Contrary to the defendants' contention, any error by the Supreme Court in issuing the order and judgment of foreclosure and sale before the defendant's time to oppose the plaintiff's motion had expired and before the return date is not the type of error contemplated by CPLR 5015(a)(4) ( see Blue Lagoon, LLC v Reisman , 214 AD3d at 942; Forest Walnut LLC v Abizker , 224 AD3d 408, 409). Accordingly, the court properly denied the defendants' motion pursuant to CPLR 5015(a)(4) to vacate the order and judgment of foreclosure and sale. 
 CONNOLLY, J.P., BRATHWAITE NELSON, LOVE and MCCORMACK, JJ., concur.

JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. v Lee 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06806 
 November 18, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 JPMorgan Chase Bank, National Association, respondent, 
 v 
 Kenneth Lee, appellant, et al., defendants. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on November 18, 2026 
 2023-06123, (Index No. 9767/09) 
 Valerie Brathwaite Nelson, J.P. 
 Deborah A. Dowling 
 Janice A. Taylor 
 Laurence L. Love, JJ. 

 Biolsi Law Group, P.C., New York, NY (Steven Alexander Biolsi of counsel), for appellant. 
 Bonchonsky & Zaino, LLP, Garden City, NY (Peter R. Bonchonsky of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action to foreclose a mortgage, the defendant Kenneth Lee appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Nassau County (David P. Sullivan, J.), entered May 24, 2023. The order denied that defendant's motion pursuant to CPLR 5015(a)(3) to vacate a judgment of foreclosure and sale of the same court (Thomas A. Adams, J.) entered June 16, 2015, and for leave to interpose an answer. 
 ORDERED that the order is affirmed, with costs. 
 The plaintiff commenced this action against the defendant Kenneth Lee (hereinafter the defendant), among others, to foreclose a mortgage on certain real property located in Nassau County. The defendant failed to timely appear or answer the complaint, and on June 16, 2015, a judgment of foreclosure and sale was entered. In January 2023, the defendant moved pursuant to CPLR 5015(a)(3) to vacate the judgment of foreclosure and sale and for leave to interpose an answer. The plaintiff opposed the motion. In an order entered May 24, 2023, the Supreme Court denied the motion. The defendant appeals. 
 "CPLR 5015(a)(3) permits the court to vacate an order on the basis of fraud, misrepresentation, or other misconduct of an adverse party" ( U.S. Bank N.A. v Carucci , 217 AD3d 894, 895 [internal quotation marks omitted]). A defendant seeking to vacate a default based on intrinsic fraud must establish a reasonable excuse for the default and a potentially meritorious defense to the action ( see HSBC Bank USA, N.A. v Goxall , 239 AD3d 714, 716; Bank of N.Y. Mellon Trust Co., N.A. v Iaboni , 230 AD3d 1204, 1206). 
 Here, the defendant's contention that the plaintiff obtained the judgment of foreclosure and sale by submitting fraudulent documents to establish its standing to commence this action amounts to an allegation of intrinsic fraud ( see U.S. Bank, N.A. v Robinson , 168 AD3d 1120, 1121; US Bank N.A. v Galloway , 150 AD3d 1174, 1175). Since the defendant failed to timely appear or answer the complaint, and thereafter failed to offer an excuse for his default, he is precluded from asserting lack of standing as a defense ( see Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v [*2] O'Connor , 223 AD3d 872, 877; Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Davis , 216 AD3d 704, 706). Moreover, RPAPL 1302-a, which allows a defendant in a foreclosure action to raise the issue of standing at any time, does not apply to a defaulting defendant ( see US Bank N.A. v Eisler , 237 AD3d 999, 1000; U.S. Bank N.A. v Goldberger , 211 AD3d 1077, 1078). 
 BRATHWAITE NELSON, J.P., DOWLING, TAYLOR and LOVE, JJ., concur.

Samson MCA, LLC v Artiles Hauling & Delivery Corp 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06843 
 November 18, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Samson MCA, LLC, respondent, 
 v 
 Artiles Hauling and Delivery Corp, etc., et al., appellants, et al., defendants. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on November 18, 2026 
 2025-05740, 2025-07679, 2025-15169, (Index No. 33086/24) 
 Francesca E. Connolly, J.P. 
 Paul Wooten 
 Janice A. Taylor 
 Lisa S. Ottley, JJ. 

 Peska & Associates, P.C., White Plains, NY (Adam M. Peska of counsel), for appellants. 
 Berkovitch & Bouskila, PLLC, Pomona, NY (Ariel Bouskila of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action, inter alia, to recover damages for breach of contract, the defendants Artiles Hauling and Delivery Corp, Artiles Hauling, Inc, Tiles Hauling, Inc, and Vicente Artiles appeal from (1) an order of the Supreme Court, Rockland County (Hal B. Greenwald, J.), dated May 7, 2025, (2) a judgment of the same court dated May 9, 2025, and (3) a money judgment of the same court dated December 8, 2025. The order, insofar as appealed from, granted that branch of the plaintiff's motion which was for summary judgment on the issue of liability against the defendants Artiles Hauling and Delivery Corp, Artiles Hauling, Inc, Tiles Hauling, Inc, and Vicente Artiles, and denied the defendants' motion for a preliminary injunction. The judgment, insofar as appealed from, upon the order, is in favor of the plaintiff and against the defendants Artiles Hauling and Delivery Corp, Artiles Hauling, Inc, Tiles Hauling, Inc, and Vicente Artiles in the total sum of $179,323.59. The money judgment, insofar as appealed from, awarded the plaintiff attorneys' fees and disbursements payable by those defendants in the total sum of $18,327.19. 
 ORDERED that the appeal from the order is dismissed; and it is further, 
 ORDERED that the judgment is affirmed insofar as appealed from; and it is further, 
 ORDERED that the money judgment is affirmed insofar as appealed from; and it is further, 
 ORDERED that one bill of costs is awarded to the plaintiff. 
 The appeal from so much of the order as denied the defendants' motion for a preliminary injunction is dismissed as academic in light of our determination on the appeal from the judgment ( see Aniqa Halal Live Poultry Corp. v Montague-Lee Ltd. Partnership , 110 AD3d 934, 935). The appeal from the remaining portions of the order must be dismissed because the right of direct appeal therefrom terminated with the entry of the judgment in the action ( see Matter of Aho , 39 NY2d 241, 248). The issues raised on the appeal from those portions of the order are brought up [*2] for review and have been considered on the appeal from the judgment ( see CPLR 5501[a][1]). 
 In June 2024, the plaintiff commenced this action, inter alia, to recover damages for breach of contract against, among others, the defendants Artiles Hauling and Delivery Corp, Artiles Hauling, Inc, Tiles Hauling, Inc (hereinafter collectively the Artiles companies), and Vicente Artiles (hereinafter Vicente), the president and chief executive officer of the Artiles companies (hereinafter collectively with the Artiles companies, the appellants). The plaintiff alleged, among other things, that the Artiles companies breached a commercial financing agreement (hereinafter the agreement), to which Vicente was a co-guarantor, by failing to remit to the plaintiff its share of future receivables due under the agreement. In an amended answer, the appellants raised, inter alia, an affirmative defense, in effect, that the agreement was, in actuality, a loan with a usurious interest rate. 
 Thereafter, the plaintiff moved for summary judgment on the complaint. The appellants opposed the motion. In an order dated May 7, 2025, the Supreme Court, inter alia, granted that branch of the plaintiff's motion which was for summary judgment on the issue of liability against the appellants. On May 9, 2025, the court issued a judgment, among other things, in favor of the plaintiff and against the appellants in the total sum of $179,323.59. In a money judgment dated December 8, 2025, the court, inter alia, awarded the plaintiff attorneys' fees and disbursements payable by the appellants in the total sum of $18,327.19. These appeals ensued. 
 On appeal, the appellants do not contest that the plaintiff established, prima facie, that the appellants breached the agreement. The appellants contend, among other things, that the Supreme Court erred by granting that branch of the plaintiff's motion which was for summary judgment on the issue of liability against them because the agreement was, in actuality, a criminally usurious loan. 
 "The rudimentary element of usury is the existence of a loan or forbearance of money, and where there is no loan, there can be no usury, however unconscionable the contract may be" ( Crystal Springs Capital, Inc. v Big Thicket Coin, LLC , 220 AD3d 745, 746 [internal quotation marks omitted]; see True Bus. Funding, LLC v Guerrero A Constr. Corp. , 239 AD3d 787, 788). "When determining whether a transaction constitutes a usurious loan[,] it must be considered in its totality and judged by its real character, rather than by the name, color, or form which the parties have seen fit to give it" ( Abir v Malky, Inc. , 59 AD3d 646, 649 [internal quotation marks omitted]; see True Bus. Funding, LLC v Guerrero A Constr. Corp. , 239 AD3d at 788; LG Funding, LLC v United Senior Props. of Olathe, LLC , 181 AD3d 664, 665). "To determine whether a transaction constitutes a usurious loan: The court must examine whether the plaintiff is absolutely entitled to repayment under all circumstances. Unless a principal sum advanced is repayable absolutely, the transaction is not a loan" ( Principis Capital, LLC v I Do, Inc. , 201 AD3d 752, 754 [internal quotation marks omitted]; see True Bus. Funding, LLC v Guerrero A Constr. Corp. , 239 AD3d at 788). "Courts generally 'weigh three factors when determining whether repayment is absolute or contingent: (1) whether there is a reconciliation provision in the agreement; (2) whether the agreement has a finite term; and (3) whether there is any recourse should the merchant declare bankruptcy'" ( True Bus. Funding, LLC v Guerrero A Constr. Corp. , 239 AD3d at 788, quoting Principis Capital, LLC v I Do, Inc. , 201 AD3d at 754; see LG Funding, LLC v United Senior Props. of Olathe, LLC , 181 AD3d at 665-666). 
 Here, the plaintiff demonstrated, prima facie, that the transaction at issue was a purchase of future receivables and not a criminally usurious loan ( see Apollo Funding Co. v Dave Reilly Constr., LLC , 241 AD3d 1508, 1509; True Bus. Funding, LLC v Guerrero A Constr. Corp. , 239 AD3d at 788). The plaintiff established that the agreement contained a clause that provided the appellants the right to request reconciliation to adjust payments in response to fluctuations in its weekly receipts and that this clause rendered the term of the agreement indefinite ( see True Bus. Funding, LLC v Guerrero A Constr. Corp. , 239 AD3d at 788). Moreover, the plaintiff established that no contractual provision existed establishing that a declaration of bankruptcy would constitute an event of default ( see Apollo Funding Co. v Dave Reilly Constr., LLC , 241 AD3d at 1509). 
 In opposition to the plaintiff's prima facie showing of entitlement to judgment as a matter of law on the issue of liability against the appellants, the appellants failed to raise a triable [*3] issue of fact. Vicente's mere averment in his affidavit that he did not sign the personal guaranty, without more, was insufficient to raise a triable issue of fact as to the validity of his personal guaranty ( see Banco Popular N. Am. v Victory Taxi Mgt. , 1 NY3d 381, 384; Sterling Natl. Bank v Alan B. Brill, P.C. , 186 AD3d 515, 518). 
 Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted that branch of the plaintiff's motion which was for summary judgment on the issue of liability against the appellants. 
 The appellants' remaining contentions are either not properly before this Court or without merit. 
 CONNOLLY, J.P., WOOTEN, TAYLOR and OTTLEY, JJ., concur.

MEMORANDUM BY BECK, J.: FILED NOVEMBER 18, 2026 
 Appellant 1726 South 5th Street Associate LLC (“the LLC”) appeals from 
the judgment entered on July 25, 2025, by the Philadelphia County Court of 
Common Pleas (“trial court”) in favor of Appellee Carolyn Claus a/k/a Carolyn 
Closs (“Closs”) and against the LLC for possession of property located at 1217 
North 15th Street in Philadelphia (“the Property”). The LLC raises the 
timeliness of Closs’ challenge to an underlying sheriff’s sale of the Property 
J-A21002-26 
- 3 - 
and further claims the trial court erred in proceeding to trial at a hearing that 
was scheduled for oral argument, depriving the LLC of its right to produce 
testimony and evidence. For the reasons that follow, we vacate the judgment 
and remand for proceedings consistent with this decision. 
 The Property is a vacant lot in the City of Philadelphia (“City”), which 
the LLC purchased for $84,000 on December 15, 2015, at a sale by the 
Philadelphia Sheriff’s Office on account of unpaid real estate taxes.1 By way 
of background, when John L. Davis died in 1983, he left the Property to his 
brother and numerous nephews, nieces, grandnephews, and grandnieces. At 
the time of the sheriff’s sale, there were 24 record owners of the Property who 
each held an interest ranging from 14.69% to 0.37%. Closs was one of 8 
owners with a 0.37% interest.2 None of the 0.37% owners were named as a 
party to the sheriff’s sale action. 
 On February 9, 2021, the LLC filed a complaint in quiet title against the 
0.37% owners, seeking to clear title to the Property for resale. None of the 
defendants, except Closs, responded. Closs filed a counseled answer, new

matter, and counterclaim on September 30, 2022. In her new matter, Closs 
averred that because she never received notice of the sheriff’s sale action and 
was not joined as a party, her interest in the Property was not divested at the 
sheriff’s sale. She counterclaimed that the sheriff’s sale action was fatally 
flawed because the City failed to identify all owners of the Property; the LLC 
negligently and recklessly relied on the actions of the City in purchasing the

 On November 16, 2022, the trial court entered default judgment against

 Before a pretrial settlement conference scheduled for September 11, 
2024, the trial court granted a motion to withdraw as counsel filed by Closs’

 On October 22, 2024, Closs filed a motion to dismiss in which she

leads.text:
IN THE COURT OF CHANCERY OF THE STATE OF DELAWARE 
PPG INDUSTRIES, INC., 
Plaintiff, 
v. 
WESTLAKE CORPORATION, AXIALL 
CORPORATION, WESTLAKE US 2 
LLC (f/k/a EAGLE US 2 LLC), and 
EAGLE SPINCO INC., 

Defendants. 

C.A. No. 2024-0648-NAC 

 POST-TRIAL MEMORANDUM OPINION 
Date Submitted: August 4, 2026 
Date Decided: November 18, 2026 
David A. Dorey, Gregory P. Ranzini , BLANK ROME LLP, Wilmington, Delaware; 
Andrew Fletcher, Jason Snyderman, John A. Gibbons, BLANK ROME LLP, 
Philadelphia, Pennsylvania; Counsel for Plaintiff and Counterclaim Defendant PPG 
Industries, Inc. 

Jennifer C. Wasson, Tyler E. Cragg, POTTER ANDERSON & CORROON LLP, 
Wilmington, Delaware; William R. H. Merrill, Ryan V. Caughey, Ace M. Factor, 
Alexxa Leon , SUSMAN GODF REY LLP, Houston, Texas; David B. Goodwin, 
Christine S. Haskett, COVINGTON & BURLING LLP, San Francisco, California; 
Counsel for Defendants and Counterclaim Plaintiffs Westlake Corporation, Axiall 
Corporation, Westlake US 2 LLC (f/k/a Eagle US 2 LLC), and Eagle Spinco Inc. 

COOK, V.C.

In 1998, cargo ship DG Harmony caught fire off the coast of Brazil. After 
attempting to fight the flames, the crew abandoned ship, and the fire destroyed the 
vessel and most of its cargo. A flurry of lawsuits followed. In a consolidated action, 
the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York found that 
calcium hypochlorite manufactured by PPG Industries, Inc. caused the fire. PPG 
settled the claims for $81.5 million, with insurance contributing $56.5 million after 
PPG satisfied a $25 million self-insured retention amount. 
In 2006, Di Gregório Navegação Ltda . (“Di Gregorio”) —a Brazilian cargo 
transportation company that sub-chartered the DG Harmony—filed a lawsuit against 
PPG in Brazil. Despite being named in the consolidated New York action, Di Gregorio 
never appeared. In 2009, the New York court entered an order of default judgment 
against Di Gregorio, specifically enjoining the Brazil lawsuit. Notwithstanding the 
New York court’s order, the Di Gregorio litigation in Brazil continued, and, in 2010, 
the Brazil court found PPG liable against Di Gregorio. 
In 2013, PPG spun off its commodity chemicals business through a transaction 
involving Georg ia Gulf Corporation, later renamed Axiall Corporation. The 
transaction was governed by a series of agreements, including a Separation 
Agreement and a Contribution Agreement. Those agreements addressed the transfer 
of assets and assumption of liabilities, the parties’ indemnification rights and 
obligations, and their rights and responsibilities concerning insurance. As relevant 
here, the Separation Agreement allocated responsibility for the Di Gregorio litigation 
2 
to entities in the spun- off business. And PPG retained the insurance policies 
potentially covering the Di Gregorio litigation. 
For years after the transaction, the spun-off entities defended the Di Gregorio 
litigation and communicated with PPG’s insurers , including submitting invoices for 
defense costs. In 2023 and 2024, the Di Gregorio litigation was coming to a head. A 
decision on damages was imminent, and everyone started taking positions. Desp ite 
years of communication —including about strategy and settlement —the insurers 
refused to engage with the spun -off entities without an assignment from PPG , and 
they denied coverage for the Di Gregorio litigation. PPG refused to assign any rights 
to the insurance until any judgment in the Di Gregorio litigation was satisfied. The 
spun-off entities demanded an assignment before they would pay anything in the Di 
Gregorio litigation. 
In May 2024, the Brazil court entered a substantial damages award against 
PPG. The next month, PPG filed this action asking the Court to order the spun- off 
entities and their subsequent acquirer (collectively, Defendants here) to substitute 
PPG out of the Di Gregorio litigation and post a bond or satisfy the judgment. 
Defendants countered, asking the Court to order PPG to assign insurance rights to 
them. 
This decision denies PPG’s requests for specific performance and grants 
Defendants’ in part. Even assuming PPG has proven a breach of contract, it has not 
shown, by clear and convincing evidence , that specific performance is appropriate . 
PPG waited to request substitution for 11 years after the spinoff, and it would violate 
3 
principles of comity for this Court to order Defendants to take any action in the Di 
Gregorio litigation when that litigation was specifically enjoined by the New York 
court’s 2009 order. Defendants are entitled to an assignment of insurance proceeds, 
but, under the Separation Agreement’s terms, only for the costs of defending PPG in 
the Di Gregorio litigation that they have already incurred and paid. 
The parties agree that the spun-off entities are ultimately responsible for any 
enforceable judgment and related losses. And Defendants continue to defend the Di 
Gregorio litigation and have committed to hold PPG harmless against any attempts 
to enforce the Di Gregorio judgment. The parties also agree that the spun-off entities 
are entitled to an assignment of insurance proceeds at some point. Boiled down, the 
parties tussle over the logistics of their contractual obligations, with the crux of th e 
dispute concerning sequencing and timing. Like colleagues arriving at the entrance 
to the office, PPG and Defendants are dancing over who goes first and who will hold 
the door. In the end, they’ll both make it inside. 
I. FACTUAL BACKGROUND 
The following facts were stipulated to by the parties or proven by a 
preponderance of the evidence at trial.1 

1 See Dkt. 147, Pre-Trial Stipulation and Order (”PTO”). The trial record includes live 
testimony from two fact witnesses and four experts, 234 joint exhibits, and three deposition 
transcripts. Trial testimony is cited as “TT [Page]:[Lines] (Name).” See Dkts. 179 –80. 
Exhibits are cited by the numbers provided on the parties’ joint exhibit list as “JX ,” unless 
otherwise defined. See Dkt. 170. Pincites refer to pagination stamped with the parties’ joint 
exhibit numbers. Deposition transcripts are cited as “[Name] Dep. [Page]:[Lines].” 
4 
A. The Parties 
Plaintiff PPG Industries, Inc. is an industrial conglomerate based in 
Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Through a Separation Agreement dated July 18, 2012, 2 
PPG agreed to spin off its commodity chemicals business in a transaction (the 
“Spinoff”) with Georg ia Gulf Corporation, which was subsequently renamed Axiall 
Corporation. 
Defendant Eagle Spinco Inc. was PPG’s counterparty to the Separation 
Agreement and is a wholly owned subsidiary of Axiall.3 
Defendant Eagle US 2 LLC (now Westlake US 2 LLC) is a subsidiary of Eagle 
Spinco.4 Eagle US 2 was a party to the Contribution Agreement dated January 22, 
2013, with PPG as its counterparty. 5 The purpose of the Contribution Agreement 
was “solely to effect the transfer of” assets and liabilities contemplated by the 
Separation Agreement.6 
Defendant Axiall Corporation is Eagle Spinco’s parent company. Axiall 
acquired Eagle Spinco in 2013. This decision refers to Axiall, Eagle US 2, and Eagle 
Spinco as the “Spinco Group.” 

2 JX 23. 
3 PTO ¶ 2. 
4 Id. ¶ 3. 
5 JX 41. 
6 Id. § 1.2. 
5 
Defendant Westlake Corporation is Axiall’s, Eagle Spinco’s, and Eagle US 2’s 
ultimate parent company. 7 Westlake acquired Axiall in 2016. 8 Westlake is not a 
party to the Separation or Contribution Agreements. This decision refers to Westlake 
and the Spinco Group as “Defendants.”9 
B. The DG Harmony Fire and Ensuing Litigation 
In November 1998 , an explosion occurred aboard the container ship DG 
Harmony off the coast of Brazil. 10 The explosion caused a total loss of the ship and 
its cargo. Among DG Harmony’s cargo was PPG -manufactured calcium 
hypochlorite. 11 Following the DG Harmony fire, numerous parties sued PPG, 
alleging that its calcium hypochlorite caused the explosion and subsequent fire. The 
claims were consolidated in the United States District Court for the Southern District 
of New York. In 2009, the court entered a judgment, finding PPG liable for the 

7 PTO ¶ 5. 
8 JX 92; JX 98. 
9 As explained below, however, the Court concludes that Westlake is not a proper 
defendant in this action. 
10 PTO ¶ 15. 
11 Id. ¶ 16. 
6 
explosion and the resulting fire. 12 PPG eventually settled the lawsuits for 
approximately $81.5 million.13 
C. The Di Gregorio Litigation 
On January 11, 2006, Di Gregório Navegação Ltda (“Di Gregorio”)—a Brazilian 
cargo transportation company that sub -chartered the DG Harmony—filed a lawsuit 
against PPG in the 13th Civil and Work Accident Court of the District of Manaus, 
State of Amazonas, Brazil (the “ Di Gregorio Litigation”).14 PPG hired the Brazilian 
law firm Mattos Filho, Veiga Filho, Marrey Jr. e Quiroga Advogados (“Mattos Filho”) 
as defense counsel in the Di Gregorio Litigation.
15 
Di Gregorio was a named party in the consolidated New York litigation but did 
not appear.16 In June 2006, PPG filed a lawsuit against Di Gregorio in the Southern 
District of New York, seeking to enjoin the Di Gregorio Litigation. 17 On October 28, 
2009, the New York court entered a default judgment in PPG’s favor, declaring that 
PPG was not liable to Di Gregorio and enjoining Di Gregorio from pursuing any

Harmony, 394 F. Supp. 2d 649 (S.D.N.Y. 2005), opinion clarified, 2007 WL 895251 (S.D.N.Y. 
Mar. 16, 2007), and aff’d in part, vacated in part, rev’d in part, 533 F.3d 83 (2d Cir. 2008). 
13 TT 162:2–10 (Bloch). 
14 PTO ¶¶ 19, 21. 
15 Id. ¶ 22; JX 10. 
16 PTO ¶ 20. 
17 JX 11. 
7 
claims against PPG for losses arising from the DG Harmony fire (the “SDNY 
Order”).18 The SDNY Order expressly enjoined the Di Gregorio Litigation.19 
Notwithstanding the SDNY Order, the Brazil court allowed the Di Gregorio 
Litigation to proceed and, in January 2010, entered judgment against PPG in the 
liability phase of the litigation. 20 PPG appealed the liability finding but was 
unsuccessful.21 
At the time of the DG Harmony fire, PPG maintained an insurance tower 
worth $350 million, subject to a $25 million self-insured retention.22 PPG notified its 
insurers about the DG Harmony fire and submitted insurance claims for liabilities 
arising from it, including the Di Gregorio Litigation. 23 Before the Separation 
Agreement was executed in 2012, PPG had received about $56.5 million in 
reimbursement from its insurance for DG Harmony-related losses.24 Just under $300

8 
million of insurance remains available under PPG’s applicable insurance policy. And 
the Di Gregorio Litigation is the only remaining open claim under that policy.25 
D. The Spinoff 
In 2012, while the Di Gregorio Litigation was proceeding, PPG agreed to spin 
off and sell its chlor -alkali, derivatives, and other commodity chemicals business to 
Georgia Gulf (now Axiall) through a series of agreements, including, as relevant here, 
the Separation Agreement and the Contribution Agreement. 
Through the Separation Agreement, PPG agreed to transfer certain assets to 
Eagle Spinco, and Eagle Spinco agreed to assume certain liabilities, with the 
remaining assets and liabilities to be retained by PPG. 26 The Contribution 
Agreement effectuated the transfer of the assets and liabilities to Eagle US 2 (an 
Eagle Spinco subsidiary) in accordance with the terms of the Separation 
Agreement.27 
Among the liabilities Eagle US 2 assumed under the Separation Agreement 
was the Di Gregorio Litigation (the “Di Gregorio Liability”) .28 According to the

Judgment rendered November 18, 2026. 
Application for rehearing may be filed 
within the delay allowed by Art. 2166, 
La. C.C.P. 

No. 57,203-CA 

COURT OF APPEAL 
SECOND CIRCUIT 
STATE OF LOUISIANA 

* * * * * 

TYLER GORDON, MICHAEL 
CRAFT, AND MARY 
BLAKEMORE 
 Plaintiffs-Appellants 

versus 

CITY OF SHREVEPORT Defendant-Appellee 

* * * * * 

Appealed from the 
First Judicial District Court for the 
Parish of Caddo, Louisiana 
Trial Court No. 661,810 

Honorable Ramon Lafitte, Judge 

* * * * * 

WALTZER WIYGUL GARSIDE & WILD Counsel for Appellants 
By: Clay Garside 

JACK BAILEY LAW CORPORATION 
By: Jack Bailey, III 

CARMOUCHE, BOKENFOHR, Counsel for Appellee 
BUCKLE & DAY, PLLC 
By: Nichole M. Buckle 

* * * * * 

Before STONE, STEPHENS, and ROBINSON, JJ.

STEPHENS, J., 
This civil appeal arises from the First Judicial District, Parish of 
Caddo, State of Louisiana, the Honorable Ramon Lafitte, Judge, presiding. 
The plaintiffs, Tyler Gordon, Michael Craft, and Mary Blakemore, have 
appealed from the trial court’s judgment affirming the Shreveport City 
Council’s decision approving a special use permit. For the reasons 
expressed below, we affirm the trial court’s judgment. 
FACTS AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY 
 On October 17, 2025, Bohler Engineering filed a development 
application with the Shreveport/Caddo Metropolitan Planning Commission 
(“MPC”), seeking a special use permit for a proposed data center. Bohler 
requested that the data center be developed on approximately 254 acres 
zoned I-1 PUD, Light Industrial Planned Unit Development (“PUD”), an 
area known as Resilient Technology Park located off Greenwood Road. The 
application requested approval for seven buildings, each measuring 400,000 
sq. ft., to be used as a data center, along with various support buildings such 
as water storage, a substation, a lift station, and offices. The Bohler Project 
Team held a community meeting about the project on November 13, 2025, 
where an open floor discussion occurred at the Bill Cockrell Community 
Center in Shreveport involving the project’s purpose, design elements, and 
anticipated timeline, as well as community considerations and feedback.1 
Following Bohler’s development application, the MPC staff issued a 
report which included findings that data centers are permitted within the I-1 

1 The staff report indicated that 11 members of the neighborhood community were 
present as well as elected officials, several members from the applicant team, and two 
MPC staff members. The community members raised concerns about the impact to the 
water and electrical supply, traffic, and noise generated by the proposed data center. Job 
creation potential and other benefits to the community were also discussed. 
2 

base zoning district, but that a special use permit is required when the site is 
located within 200 feet of a residentially zoned district. The report described 
that the proposed site at Resilient Technology Park was rezoned on several 
occasions and had previous plan approvals for various developments, but 
these prior developments never occurred.2 The report also detailed that the 
proposed site abuts residentially zoned districts on the north and east sides; 
therefore, a special use permit application was required. The MPC staff 
explained that the closest residential dwelling is approximately 250 feet 
from the property boundary of the proposed site. The MPC staff report 
ultimately concluded that the proposed development properly mitigated the 
impact of the proposed use, and approval was warranted. In the report, all 
12 criteria of development standards and design specifications were deemed 
satisfied as follows: 
Section 16.3.E.1: the design, location, and operating plans of an SUP 
must be such that the public health, safety and/or welfare is protected. 
Since the property in question is part of a PUD, the site plan 
incorporates several amenities beyond the minimum requirements 
of the code that are intended to protect the public health, safety, and 
welfare of the surrounding property owners. The amenities are as 
follows: a. Two dense wooded buffers located throughout the site to 
shield surrounding properties from activities at the site, including: (1) 

2 The MPC staff report detailed the zoning history as follows: 

“In 1990, the rear portion of this site was rezoned from R-A to I-2 and 
received site plan approval for industrial manufacturing, warehouse & 
distribution (C-55-90). There was a stipulation to revert to R-A if 
development did not occur. The property reverted to R-A due to this 
stipulation. In 2011, the entire lot was rezoned from R-A to R-A-E, 
Rural Ag Extended Use for a proposed warehouse and distribution 
center. Again, development did not occur, and the zoning reverted to 
R-A (C-76-11). In 2016, the property was rezoned from R-A to I-1 
(PUD). If development didn’t occur within 2 years, then the only 
thing that expired was the preliminary plat. The PUD designation 
stayed, along with all stipulations and public amenities. Development 
did not occur within two years, and the preliminary site plan expired. 
The I-1 PUD designation remained. (C-6-16). In 2020, a new 
preliminary site plan was approved for a SWEPCO transmission 
control center. (20-197-C).” 
3 

A 150’ wide forested buffer separating the proposed development 
from the residentially zoned property along its western and northern 
boundaries shall be maintained and preserved; and (2) A wooded 
buffer of an undetermined size at the southern end (front) of the 
property to separate it from the existing B-S and I-1 uses along 
Greenwood Rd. shall likewise be maintained and preserved; b. Tree 
preservation at the site which will leave a substantial wooded area 
along the south eastern boundary and serves to separate the property 
from the existing I.1 use adjacent to the site; c. Use of building 
materials with high solar reflexive indices to minimize heat island 
effect; d. Additional landscaping will be provided at the site of the 
detention ponds; and e. Signage at the site will be limited to 
monument and architectural signage styles. 

Section 16.3.E.2: the proposed special use is compatible with the 
general land use of adjacent properties and other property within 300 
feet. The proposed building area is situated more than 500 feet from 
the nearest residential dwelling, providing a substantial spatial 
buffer between the use and surrounding neighborhoods mitigating 
potential land-use conflicts. The site contains mature vegetation along 
its perimeter, which the applicant intends to retain in order to preserve 
existing visual screening and reduce potential impacts. Due to the 
sites proximity to an interstate and a major highway, ambient noise 
levels in the area are already elevated; therefore, noise generated by 
the data center’s operations is not anticipated to exceed existing 
background conditions. Additionally, the proposed use is 
characterized by low trip generation and is not expected to produce 
traffic volumes that would negatively affect adjacent roadways or 
residential areas. Based on the site’s layout, the retention of existing 
buffers, and the low-intensity operational characteristics of the use, 
the proposed development is expected to be compatible with 
surrounding land uses. 

Section 16.3.E.3: the special use conforms to the regulations of the 
zoning district where it will be located. The proposal exceeds the 
zoning district regulations and all amenities from the approved PUD 
are met, as proposed in the site plan. 

Section 16.3.E.4: the location and dimensions of all public rights-of-
way on or abutting the proposed special use. Primary access to the 
site will be from Resilient Way, which is a recently constructed public 
dedication that also serves the SWEPCO transmission control center. 
Future access to the site is proposed from Bert Kouns Industrial Loop, 
which is currently undeveloped. The site plan proposes a future 
extension of the Industrial Loop; however, this will require separate 
approval from the subject application. A traffic impact study will be 
required prior to the release a building permit. It’s important to note 
4 

that a traffic impact study will not determine whether a land use 
should be denied or not, rather it will determine if changes to the right 
of way are necessary to accommodate the proposed use. 

Section l6.3.E.5: existing and proposed vehicular and pedestrian 
circulation systems; including streets, alleys, walkways, service areas 
and loading areas, the location and arrangement of off-street parking 
areas and all points of vehicular entrance and exit. Off-street vehicle 
parking is no longer required to meet a specific minimum ratio 
following the adoption of the recent parking reform code text 
amendment. The applicant has proposed 750 vehicle parking spaces, 
which they indicate is necessary to support the needs of the facility. 
This should not be interpreted as representing the total number of 
vehicles expected to be on site at any given time. As indicated, this is 
a low traffic generating use; however, due to the scale of the overall 
development, each building requires an adequate supply of parking 
spaces, resulting in a higher cumulating parking count. 

In terms of site access, the primary driveway on Resilient Way is 
situated at the far northern end of the property. This configuration 
allows vehicles entering the site to be fully removed from Greenwood 
Road, minimizing the potential for vehicle stacking or congestion 
along the roadway that could interfere with other motorists. The 
traffic impact study will reveal whether further mitigation is 
warranted. 

Section 16.3.E.6: the outdoor surfacing end paving for all parking 
and loading areas. The outdoor parking areas will comprise of heavy-
duty concrete, meeting the code requirements. 

Section 16.3.E.7: the proposed perimeter treatment of the property, 
with indication of screening materials to be used, including fences, 
walls, and plants: together with a description of uses, setbacks and 
the relationship to surrounding areas. Section 16.3.E.8: a landscape 
plan showing proposed treatment of the areas designated as either 
buffers or open space. As required by the 2016 PUD approval, a 150’ 
buffer yard will be preserved at the northern boundary of the site 
where it abuts undeveloped residentially zoned property. On the 
eastern portion of the site, the proposed buildings will be situated 
approximately 443’ from the adjacent undeveloped residential parcel. 
While the UDC requires a minimum buffer yard of 30’ when an 
industrial district abutting residential, the site plan shows that existing 
vegetation at a depth of approximately 300’ will remain on the east 
property boundary and 150’ on the north boundary. Given the 
proximity to residentially zoned land, these areas warrant heightened 
sensitivity with respect to the impact of the proposed use. The 
additional vegetated buffer significantly exceeds minimum 
5 

requirements and provides appropriate mitigation between the 
proposed industrial use and the adjoining residential properties. 

Section 16.3.E.9: the location and dimensions of all existing and 
proposed easements and public improvements on the site. The City of 
Shreveport Public Works Department has reviewed the plans. There 
are no known easements or public improvements on site. 

Section 16.3.E.10: the location and size of all structures, distances 
between buildings, and distances from structures to property lines. 
Section 16.3.E.12: the proposed use of all structures and their 
dimensions, i.e., height, floor areas, entrances, and loading areas. As 
previously indicated, there is substantial distance of the proposed 
buildings to the property lines, mitigating the impact of the use. Each 
building will be 400,000 sf in area and is sited at the interior portions
