leads.caseName: Futurewise v. Kitsap County
leads.text:
IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF THE STATE OF WASHINGTON 

DIVISION II 

FUTUREWISE, No. 61665-3-II 

 Appellant, 

 v. 

KITSAP COUNTY, and the STATE OF UNPUBLISHED OPINION 
WASHINGTON, GROWTH 
MANAGEMENT HEARINGS BOARD, 

 Respondents. 

MAXA, P.J. – Futurewise appeals a Final Decision and Order of the Growth Management 
Hearings Board (the Board) dismissing one of its challenges to Kitsap County’s 2024 
amendments to its comprehensive plan and certain development regulations. This administrative 
appeal arose from Futurewise’s argument that Kitsap County (the County) was required but 
failed to revise its comprehensive plan and development regulations to protect surface and 
groundwater as required by various statutes, including RCW 36.70A.590. 
 The Growth Management Act (GMA), chapter 36.70A RCW, requires counties to create a 
comprehensive plan to guide their land use and development decision making. The GMA also 
requires counties to enact development regulations that implement and are consistent with the 
Filed 
Washington State 
Court of Appeals 
Division Two 

November 17, 2026 
No. 61665-3-II 
2 
comprehensive plan. Comprehensive plans and development regulations are subject to 
continuing review and evaluation. 
 The County conducted a periodic review and amended its comprehensive plan in 2016. 
In January 2018, the legislature enacted RCW 36.70A.590, which states that a county “may rely 
on or refer to applicable minimum instream flow rules” to comply with the provisions of the 
GMA relating to surface and groundwater resources, and that “[d]evelopment regulations must 
ensure proposed water uses are consistent with” certain other statutes involving water use. 
 In February 2018, the County enacted Ordinance 551-2018, a development regulation. 
Ordinance 551-2018 requires building permit applicants to produce evidence of water 
availability in the building permitting process. In 2024, the County conducted another periodic 
review and enacted Ordinance 637-2024, which updated the County’s comprehensive plan and 
certain development regulations. 
 Futurewise filed a petition for review to the Board challenging various aspects of the 
County’s 2024 amendments to its comprehensive plan and development regulations in Ordinance 
637-2024. Among other issues, in what the Board referred to as Issue 13, Futurewise argued that 
during its periodic review the County was required to but failed to (1) limit withdrawals of water 
from permit exempt water wells to 5,000 gallons per day and (2) improve the environment by 
enacting water regulations. Futurewise’s petition for review did not challenge Ordinance 551-
2018. 
The County responded that it was not required to update its water regulations in 
Ordinance 637-2024 because Ordinance 551-2018 already had responded to the GMA 
amendments regarding water regulations. In reply, Futurewise argued that Ordinance 551-2018 
did not bring the County into compliance with RCW 36.70A.590. 
No. 61665-3-II 
3 
 Regarding Issue 13, the Board declined to address Ordinance 551-2018 and summarily 
dismissed Futurewise’s water regulation challenge to Ordinance 637-2024 without discussion or 
analysis. 
 We hold that (1) the Board erred in refusing to address Ordinance 551-2018 because the 
County asserted that ordinance as a defense to Futurewise’s challenge to Ordinance 637-2024, 
and (2) the Board failed to decide all issues requiring resolution of Futurewise’s challenge to 
Ordinance 637-2024. Accordingly, we vacate the discussion of Issue 13 in the Board’s Final 
Decision and Order and remand to the Board for further proceedings regarding that issue. 
FACTS 
GMA Background 

 The GMA requires counties to adopt a comprehensive plan and adopt development 
regulations that are consistent with and implement the comprehensive plan. RCW 
36.70A.040(3)(d). A comprehensive plan is a “generalized coordinated land use policy statement 
of the governing body of a county or city.” RCW 36.70A.030(9). Comprehensive plans must 
include a land use element that provides for the protection of the quality and quantity of 
groundwater used for public water supplies, and a rural element that protects surface water and 
groundwater resources. RCW 36.70A.070(1), (5)(c)(iv). 
Development regulations are “the controls placed on development or land use activities 
by a county or city, including, but not limited to, zoning ordinances, critical areas ordinances, 
shoreline master programs, official controls, planned unit development ordinances, subdivision 
ordinances, and binding site plan ordinances together with any amendments thereto.” RCW 
36.70A.030(14). 
 RCW 36.70A.130(1)(a) states that a county “shall take legislative action to review and, if 
needed, revise its comprehensive land use plan and development regulations to ensure the plan 
No. 61665-3-II 
4 
and regulations comply with the requirements of [the GMA]” before certain deadlines in the 
statute. This section required the County to take action to review its comprehensive plan and 
development regulations in both 2016 and 2024. RCW 36.70A.130(4)(b), (5)(a). “Legislative 
action means the adoption of a resolution or ordinance . . . indicating at a minimum, a finding 
that a review and evaluation has occurred and identifying the revisions made, or that a revision 
was not needed and the reasons therefor.” RCW 36.70A.130(1)(c). 
The County’s Comprehensive Planning and Development Regulations 

 In 2016, the County conducted a periodic review and updated its comprehensive plan and 
development regulations, as required by RCW 36.70A.130(4)(b). But in January 2018, the 
legislature enacted RCW 36.70A.590, which states, 
For the purposes of complying with the requirements of [the GMA] relating to 
surface and groundwater resources, a county or city may rely on or refer to 
applicable minimum instream flow rules adopted by the department of ecology 
under chapters 90.22 and 90.54 RCW. Development regulations must ensure that 
proposed water uses are consistent with RCW 90.44.050 and with applicable rules 
adopted pursuant to chapters 90.22 and 90.54 RCW when making decisions under 
RCW 19.27.097 and 58.17.110. 

 In February 2018, the County enacted Ordinance 551-2018, which addressed 
requirements associated with water availability in the building permitting process. Ordinance 
551-2018 added provisions requiring a building permit applicant to provide evidence of an 
adequate water supply. Specifically, Ordinance 551-2018 stated that when a building site is 
“supplied by a permit exempt well constructed on or after January 19, 2018 . . . [t]he annual 
average withdrawal is limited to nine hundred fifty (950) gallons per day per connection for 
domestic use.” Admin. Rec. (AR) at 3165. 
In 2023, the legislature amended RCW 36.70A.020(10), adding “and enhance” to goal 10 
of the GMA, which now states, “Protect and enhance the environment and enhance the state’s 
No. 61665-3-II 
5 
high quality of life, including air and water quality, and the availability of water.” (Emphasis 
added.) 
In 2024, the County conducted a periodic review and enacted Ordinance 637-2024. 
Ordinance 637-2024 adopted an updated comprehensive plan and amended certain development 
regulations. 
Procedural History 
 Futurewise filed a petition for review to the Board challenging Ordinance 637-2024. 
Among other issues, Futurewise’s petition posed the following question as an issue presented for 
review (referred to as Issue 13): 
Did the adoption of Ordinance No. 637 -2024, the comprehensive plan, the 
Comprehensive Plan Land Use Map, Title 16 (Land Division and Development), 
and Title 17 (Zoning), protect surface and ground water as required by RCW 
36.70A.020(10), RCW 36.70A.070, RC W 36.70A.070(1), RCW 
36.70A.070(5)(c)(iv), RCW 36.70A.130(1) and (5)(a), RCW 36.70A.290(2), or 
RCW 36.70A.590? 

AR at 609.1 Futurewise’s petition did not challenge Ordinance 551-2018. 
 The Board consolidated Futurewise’s petition with other challenges to Ordinance 637-
2024. 
 Futurewise argued that the updated comprehensive plan and development regulations did 
not comply with RCW 36.70A.590 because none of its provisions limited withdrawals of water 
from permit exempt water wells to 5,000 gallons per day as required by that statute. Futurewise 
contended that because the comprehensive plan and development regulations “did not require 
compliance with applicable minimum instream flow rules” as discussed by RCW 36.70A.590, it 
violated the GMA provisions that require a comprehensive plan to include elements that protect 

1 Futurewise asserted other challenges to Ordinance 637-2024 before the Board. Those 
challenges are not at issue in this appeal. 
No. 61665-3-II 
6 
surface and groundwater resources. AR at 1977-78. Futurewise also argued that Ordinance 637-
2024 violated the amended RCW 36.70A.020(10) “[b]y failing to improve land use regulations 
to protect hydrology.” AR at 1977. 
 In addition, Futurewise argued that Ordinance 637-2024 failed to comply with (1) RCW 
36.70A.070(1),which requires that “[t]he land use element shall provide for protection of the 
quality and quantity of groundwater used for public water supplies”; and (2) RCW 
36.70A.070(5)(c)(iv), which requires that “[t]he rural element shall include measures that apply 
to rural development and protect the rural character of the area, as established by the county, by: 
. . . Protecting surface water and groundwater resources.” AR at 1977-78. 
 The County responded that it was not required to revise its comprehensive plan and 
development regulations in response to RCW 36.70A.590 and RCW 36.70A.020(10) during its 
periodic update because it already had brought itself into compliance with those regulations by 
enacting Ordinance 551-2018. In addition, the County argued that RCW 36.70A.590 did not 
require it to incorporate minimum instream flow rules under chapters 90.22 and 90.54 RCW 
because it merely stated that the county “may rely on or refer” to those rules. AR at 2289. 
Further, the County stated that the development regulations enacted by Ordinance 551-2018 
complied with RCW 36.70A.590 because they incorporated the requirements for obtaining a 
permit exempt well found in RCW 90.94.030(4)(a)(iv)(B). 
 At the hearing on the merits of Futurewise’s petition, the County also argued that 
Futurewise’s challenge to Ordinance 551-2018 was time barred. Futurewise responded that 
because the County failed to produce a publication date for Ordinance 551-2018, it could not 
establish that the statute of limitations period to challenge an ordinance under the GMA had run. 
And Futurewise emphasized that Ordinance 551-2018 did not comply with RCW 36.70A.590 
No. 61665-3-II 
7 
because it did not limit withdrawals from wells constructed before 2018 at all and did not limit 
withdrawals from permit exempt wells to 5,000 gallons per day. 
 The Board’s Final Decision and Order include a section regarding Issue 13. The Board 
recounted the parties’ arguments regarding Issue 13 and then stated, 
The Board would not anticipate the Index of Record in this matter to include the 
publication from a 2018 Ordinance, nor would the County presume to include it as 
the Issue deals with Ordinance No. 637-2024, and not Ordinance 551-2018. Thus, 
the Board is not persuaded by Futurewise’s argument regarding the 2018 Ordinance 
and find[s] issues related to that Ordinance would not be properly before this Board 
in this matter. Futurewise has not convinced this Board that this Ordinance is 
clearly erroneous. Accordingly, issue 13 is dismissed. 

AR at 3240. 
 Futurewise filed a motion for reconsideration regarding Issue 13. Futurewise argued that 
(1) the Board committed an error of fact by finding that the need for a notice of publication of 
Ordinance 551-2018 was unanticipated, (2) that the Board committed an error of law by 
implicitly concluding that the challenge to Ordinance 551-2018 was time barred

leads.caseName: HSBC Bank USA, N.A. v. Cline
leads.text:
[Cite as HSBC Bank USA, N.A. v. Cline, 2026-Ohio-4552.] 

THE COURT OF APPEALS OF OHIO 

TENTH APPELLATE DISTRICT 

HSBC Bank USA, N.A., : 

 Plaintiff-Appellee, : 
 No. 25AP-471 
v. : (C.P.C. No. 24CV-3309) 

Santana Cline a.k.a. Santana Dials et al., : (REGULAR CALENDAR) 

 Defendants-Appellants. : 

D E C I S I O N 

Rendered on November 17, 2026 
 ______ 

On brief: Laura C. Infante and Ashley E. Mueller, for appellee. 

On brief: Helen Dials, pro se. 
 ______ 
APPEAL from the Franklin County Court of Common Pleas 
MENTEL, J. 
{¶ 1} Non-party appellant, Helen Dials, appeals from a judgment of the Franklin 
County Court of Common Pleas denying her motion to intervene in a foreclosure action and 
denying as moot her motion to add herself as a party to the action. For the reasons that 
follow, we affirm the trial court’s decision. 
I. FACTS AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY 
{¶ 2} The present case was initiated on April 24, 2024, when plaintiff-appellee, 
HSBC Bank USA, N.A. (“HSBC Bank”), as Trustee on behalf of ACE Securities Corporation 
Home Equity Loan Trust and for the registered holders of ACE Securities Corporation 
Home Equity Loan Trust, Series 2006 -ASAP3, Asset Backed Pass -Through Certificates, 
filed a complaint seeking to foreclose on the real property located at 8243 Chippenham 
Drive, Dublin, Ohio 43216 (“the Property”). HSBC Bank named as defendants all parties 
who may have a legal interest in the Property, including the record title holder of the 
Property, Santana Cline a.k.a. Santana Dials (“Cline”), state and local taxing authorities, 
No. 24AP-471 2 

and specific entities with liens on the Property. (Apr. 24, 2024 Compl., generally; Ex. E.) 
In its complaint, HSBC Bank alleged that it was entitled to enforce a promissory note and 
a subsequent loan modification agreement that increased the original loan amount, the 
payment of which was secured by a mortgage on the Property. 
{¶ 3} HSBC Bank attached to its complaint as exhibits the original promissory 
note, loan modification agreement, and mortgage, each of which purportedly bears Cline’s 
signature as the promisor and mortgagor, respectively. HSBC Bank further alleged that, as 
a result of nonpayment, the note was in default and all conditions precedent to foreclosure, 
as set forth in the note and mortgage, had been satisfied. 
{¶ 4} In its complaint, HSBC Bank acknowledged that Cline had been discharged 
in bankruptcy. Accordingly, HSBC Bank did not seek a money judgment on the note but, 
instead, sought to enforce its mortgage lien through foreclosure on the Property. 
{¶ 5} At the outset of the proceedings, HSBC Bank informed the trial court that 
Cline had been declared a vexatious litigator by the Franklin County Court of Common 
Pleas on July 19, 2023, due to her conduct in prior litigation involving the Property. The 
trial court nevertheless determined that Cline retained the right to file responsive pleadings 
in the present foreclosure action. 
{¶ 6} Cline subsequently filed a pro se motion to dismiss the complaint, which the 
trial court denied. She thereafter filed a pro se answer. 
{¶ 7} On April 24, 2025, Dials, Cline’s mother, filed a motion to intervene , 
pursuant to Civ.R. 24(A) and/or Civ.R. 24(B), and a motion to add herself as a pro se party. 
In her motion, Dials argued that she had an interest in the subject matter of the action and 
should be permitted to intervene because she serves as a “Co-Power of Attorney” to Cline 
and is the “successor [t]rustee” under a trust covering the Property. (Mot. to Intervene at 
1.) In her motion to add a pro se party, Dials asserted that she should be added as a pro se 
party so as to receive notice of filings in the matter. 
{¶ 8} On May 15, 2025, the trial court issued a n order denying the motion to 
intervene and finding the motion to add a pro se party moot. The court determined that 
the record contained no evidence establishing that Dials held a Power of Attorney for Cline. 
The court further explained that, even if Dials were Cline’s alleged Power of Attorney, that 
status alone would not confer a right to intervene or authorize her to act as Cline’s legal 
No. 24AP-471 3 

representative in the proceedings. Additionally, the court found that Dials had presented 
no evidence demonstrating that the property had ever been titled in the name of the trust. 
The court further noted that, even assuming the Property had been transferred to the trust, 
Dials claimed only to be a successor trustee, rather than the trust’s current trustee. 
Accordingly, the court concluded that Dials had no present interest in the property. 
{¶ 9} Dials now appeals from that order and, in doing so, raises the following three 
assignments of error: 
1. The trial court abused its discretion by denying Appellant, as 
successor trustee and legal representative of the Trust, the right to 
intervene in this foreclosure action, despite holding a direct, 
substantial, and protectable interest in the property, i n violation of 
Ohio Civ.R. 24(A)(2) and due process. 

2. The trial court abused its discretion by removing or ignoring 
material docket entries, including the May 5 th docket, thereby 
preventing consideration of critical evidence regarding the Trust’s 
ownership and procedural history, and compromising the integrity 
of the record. 

3. The trial court abused its discretion by engaging in ex parte 
communications with the Plaintiff and its assistants, demonstrating 
bias and violating Appellant’s due process rights by prejudicing the 
Trust’s legal interests. 

II. DISCUSSION 
{¶ 10} This court reviews the denial of a motion to intervene for an abuse of 
discretion. State ex rel. N.G. v. Cuyahoga Cty. Court of Common Pleas , Juvenile Div., 
2016-Ohio-1519, ¶ 21, citing State ex rel. Merrill v. Ohio Dept. of Natural Resources, 2011-
Ohio-4612, ¶ 41. “An abuse of discretion connotes a decision that is unreasonable, 
arbitrary, or unconscionable.” H.C. v. C.P. , 2026 -Ohio-33, ¶ 6 (10th Dist.), citing 
Blakemore v. Blakemore, 5 Ohio St.3d 217, 219 (1983). 
{¶ 11} In her first assignment of error , Dials argues that the trial court abused its 
discretion in denying her motion to intervene and motion to add herself as a party. We note 
that in her original motion, Dials argued that she should be permitted to intervene under 
Civ.R. 24(A), which governs intervention as of right, and/or Civ.R. 24(B) , which governs 
permissive intervention. On appeal, however, Dials focuses her arguments only on her 
No. 24AP-471 4 

alleged right to intervene under Civ.R. 24(A). Accordingly, we will focus our analysis of the 
trial court’s denial of the motion on Civ.R. 24(A). Civ.R. 24(A) provides in relevant part: 
Upon timely application anyone shall be permitted to intervene in an 
action: . . . when the applicant claims an interest relating to the property 
or transaction that is the subject of the action and the applicant is so 
situated that the disposition of the action may as a practical matter 
impair or impede the applicant’s ability to protect that interest, unless 
the applicant’s interest is adequately represented by existing parties. 
{¶ 12} As she did in her motion to intervene, on appeal, Dials argues that she should 
be permitted to intervene as of right, under Civ.R. 24(A), because (1) she is Cline’s Power 
of Attorney, and (2) she is the successor trustee of a trust that allegedly holds title to the 
Property subject to foreclosure in this action. We agree with the trial court that neither of 
these contentions has merit. 
{¶ 13} To begin, the record does not reflect that Dials is Cline’s Power of Attorney. 
In her motion to intervene, Dials pointed to exhibits attached to Cline’s December 18, 2024 
motion to dismiss as evidence of her Power of Attorney. However, those documents do not 
show that Dials holds a Power of Attorney for Cline; rather, they purport to show that a 
person named “Timothy Dials” is Cline’s Power of Attorney. 
{¶ 14} Furthermore, there is no evidence in the record showing that a trust holds 
title to the Property subject to foreclosure in this case. Rather, the only evidence of title 
ownership is that found in Schedule B of the Preliminary Judicial Report attached as 
Exhibit E to HSBC Bank’s foreclosure complaint. That document shows that Cline is the 
sole holder of the title to the Property. Nevertheless, even if this court were to assume, for 
the sake of argument, that a trust did hold title to the Property, the only trust document in 
the record relied upon by Dials in her arguments states that Dials is merely a successor 
trustee of the trust, not the current trustee. Accordingly, the trust document does not show 
that Dials has a present legal interest in the property. 
{¶ 15} An applicant seeking intervention bears the burden of establishing the right 
to intervene. See ICSC Partners, L.P. v. Kenwood Plaza, L.P., 116 Ohio App.3d 278, 282 
(1st Dist. 1996). An applicant’s mere assertion of a claimed interest in the subject of an 
action will not suffice to permit intervention in the action under Civ.R. 24(A) ; rather, 
evidence of a claimed legal interest is necessary. See In re M.N., 2008-Ohio-3049 (9th 
Dist.). Accordingly, because Dials has failed to present the trial court with evidence of a 
No. 24AP-471 5 

legal interest related to the Property subject to foreclosure, we overrule Dials’ first 
assignment of error. 
{¶ 16} We decline to review Dials’ second and third assignments of error which 
allege, respectively, that the trial court abused its discretion in removing or ignoring docket 
entrees and abused its discretion by engaging in ex parte communications. These 
assignments of error do not touch on the trial court’s denial of the motion to intervene , 
which is the only concern on appeal at this stage. See Cline v. Wedgewood Hills HOA , 
2024-Ohio-2179, ¶ 18 (10th Dist.) (“When a non-party seeking to intervene under Civ.R. 24 
is denied intervention, their appeal is limited to the issue of intervention.”). 
III. CONCLUSION 
{¶ 17} For the foregoing reasons, we overrule Dials’ first assignment of error and 
decline to review her second and third assignments of error. The Franklin County Court of 
Common Pleas’ denial of Dials’ motion to intervene and motion to add a party is affirmed. 
Judgment affirmed. 
EDELSTEIN and DINGUS, JJ., concur. 
_____________

leads.caseName: Liberty Auto Sales, LLC v. Michael Paul Shanks
leads.text:
COURT OF APPEALS OF VIRGINIA 
Record No. 0909-25-2 
LIBERTY AUTO SALES, LLC, ET AL. 
v. 
MICHAEL PAUL SHANKS 
Present: Judges Athey, White and Senior Judge Petty 
Argued at Richmond, Virginia 
Opinion Issued November 17, 2026* 
FROM THE CIRCUIT COURT OF SPOTSYLVANIA COUNTY 
William E. Glover, Judge 

Zachary D. Crimmins (Robert J. Barlow; Marc R. Thomas; Barlow & Thomas, P.C., on brief), for 
appellants. 
(Jason M. Pelt; Norton Pelt PLC, on brief), for appellee. Appellee submitting on brief. 
MEMORANDUM OPINION BY 
JUDGE KIMBERLEY SLAYTON WHITE 
 Liberty Auto Sales, LLC and Edwin O. Paz (herein after collectively “Liberty”) appeal 
the trial court’s orders denying two motions to set aside a default judgment entered against them 
in the unlawful detainer action brought by Michael Paul Shanks. Liberty asserts that Shanks 
obtained the default judgment by fraud and that Paz was improperly served. We lack jurisdiction 
over the trial court’s order denying the motion for improper service because the notice of appeal 
was untimely. Rule 5A:6(a). Accordingly, for reasons stated in writing and filed with the 
record, the Court is of opinion that the notice of appeal was not timely filed with regard to the 
October 21, 2024 order denying the motion to vacate the default judgment for improper service. 
The Court is further of opinion that there is no error in that part of the appeal with regard to the 

* This opinion is not designated for publication. See Code § 17.1-413(A). 
 - 2 - 
order entered by the trial court on April 29, 2025, refusing to set aside the judgment. Therefore, 
we affirm in part and dismiss in part. 
BACKGROUND1 
On March 26, 2024, Shanks filed an unlawful detainer action in Spotsylvania Circuit Court 
(trial court) against Liberty for possession of a commercial property, alleging that Liberty had failed 
to pay rent and attached the lease agreement as an exhibit to the complaint. A week later, the 
Stafford County Sheriff’s Office personally served Paz as the LLC’s registered agent at an address 
in Fredericksburg. After 63 days without answer by Paz or the LLC, Shanks moved for default 
judgment. He mailed a copy of the notice and motion to Liberty at the Fredericksburg address on 
May 22, 2024. Shanks also filed a notarized affidavit affirming that the attached lease agreement 
was accurate. 
On June 17, 2024, the trial court granted default judgment, finding that Liberty had failed to 
file a timely responsive pleading despite receiving notice of the proceedings. The trial court granted 
Shanks possession of the premises and entered a $26,401 judgment against Liberty jointly and 
severally with interest, attorney fees, and costs. Although the order resolved the dispute, it stated 
that the “case is not ended at this time.” Shanks filed a request for writ of eviction, which the 
Spotsylvania County Sheriff’s Office served on June 28, 2024. 
On July 2, 2024, Paz filed, by special appearance, a motion to set aside, arguing that the 
judgment was void for improper service. The trial court suspended the eviction and directed the 
parties to appear on the motion to set aside. After a hearing, the trial court denied the motion, 

1 “On appeal, we view the evidence ‘in the light most favorable to the prevailing party 
below and its evidence is afforded all reasonable inferences fairly deducible therefrom.’” Bedell 
v. Price, 70 Va. App. 497, 500-01 (2019) (quoting Bristol Dep’t of Soc. Servs. v. Welch, 64 
Va. App. 34, 40 (2014)). 
 - 3 - 
finding that “the service of process requirements had been observed” and any service defects were 
cured under Code § 8.01-288. The trial court entered a denial order on October 21, 2024. 
Several months later, Liberty again moved the trial court to set aside the default judgment 
entered under Code § 8.01-428(A)(i), this time arguing that Shanks had procured the judgment by 
fraud on the court. Liberty asserted that the lease agreement attached to the complaint was not a 
lease between the named parties and that it was unsigned, and so the default judgment based on 
these falsehoods should be set aside. After a hearing, the trial court denied Liberty’s motion to set 
aside default judgment. In a short two-sentence order entered on April 29, 2025, the trial court ruled 
that “[u]pon the arguments presented, it is hereby: ADJUDGED, ORDERED and DECREED that 
Defendants’ ‘Motion to Set Aside Default Judgement’ be, and it hereby is, denied.” Liberty noted 
an appeal on May 29, 2025, challenging both of the trial court’s orders, one entered on October 21, 
2024, and one entered on April 29, 2025, refusing to set aside the judgment. 
ANALYSIS 
I. We lack jurisdiction to review the October 21, 2024 order. 
 “Before addressing the merits of an appeal, we first must determine whether we have 
jurisdiction.” Minor v. Commonwealth, 66 Va. App. 728, 737 (2016). “Except as otherwise 
provided by statute, no appeal will be allowed unless, within 30 days after entry of final judgment 
or other appealable order or decree, . . . counsel files with the clerk of the trial court a notice of 
appeal” and provides a copy of the notice to opposing counsel. Rule 5A:6(a) (emphasis added); see 
also Code § 8.01-675.3 (providing that “a notice of appeal to the Court of Appeals in any case 
within the jurisdiction of the court shall be filed within 30 days from the date of any final judgment 
order, decree, or conviction”). “[F]iling a timely notice of appeal is a mandatory prerequisite to an 
appellate court acquiring jurisdiction.” Ghameshlouy v. Commonwealth, 279 Va. 379, 390 (2010) 
(citing Super Fresh Food Mkts. of Va., Inc. v. Ruffin, 263 Va. 555, 563 (2002)). “[D]ismissal of an 
 - 4 - 
untimely appeal is not merely a mechanical application of a technical rule to deprive a litigant of the 
right to appeal, rather ‘[t]he purpose of the specific time limit [for filing a notice of appeal] is not to 
penalize the appellant but to protect the appellee.’” Id. at 391 (second and third alterations in 
original) (quoting Avery v. Cnty. Sch. Bd. of Brunswick Cnty., 192 Va. 329, 333 (1951)). 
“‘To determine the timeliness of a notice of appeal from a final judgment, obviously it is 
first necessary to determine the date of the action of the trial court that constitutes the final 
judgment,’ which is generally marked by the entry of a final order.” Jefferson v. Commonwealth, 
298 Va. 473, 475 (2020) (quoting Super Fresh, 263 Va. at 560). “A final order or decree . . . ‘is one 
which disposes of the whole subject, gives all of the relief contemplated . . . and leaves nothing to be 
done in the cause save to superintend ministerially the execution of the order.’” Johnson v. 
Johnson, 72 Va. App. 771, 781 (2021) (second alteration in original) (quoting Friedman v. Smith, 
68 Va. App. 529, 538 (2018)); see also Rule 1:1(b) (same). 
The trial court’s June 17, 2024 order disposed of the unlawful detainer action by ordering a 
judgment against Liberty and awarding Shanks attorney fees, costs, and possession of the premises.2 
Liberty did not appeal the default judgment. 
On July 2, 2024, Paz moved to void the default judgment for improper service. The trial 
court denied the motion to vacate on October 21, 2024. That order constituted a final order under 
Rule 1:1(b) because it resolved the motion to vacate, the only matter then pending. Johnson, 72 
Va. App. at 781. Liberty therefore had 30 days from October 21, 2024, or until November 20, 
2024, to appeal the trial court’s denial of the motion to vacate based on assertedly improper service. 

2 Although the order stated that the matter was “not ended at this time,” “a mere indication 
that the trial court intends to rule on pending motions is insufficient to negate the finality of an order 
rendering a final judgment on the merits of a case.” Carrithers v. Harrah, 60 Va. App. 69, 75 
(2012). Regardless, the trial court had limited authority to address Liberty’s motions to set aside for 
improper service and fraud under Code § 8.01-428(A). Sauder v. Ferguson, 289 Va. 449, 459 
(2015). “[S]uch jurisdiction is limited to the specific subjects set forth in paragraphs (A), (B), (C), 
or (D) of Code § 8.01-428.” State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co. v. Remley, 270 Va. 209, 221 (2005). 
 - 5 - 
But Liberty failed to note its appeal until May 29, 2025, well beyond the 30-day deadline. 
Therefore, we have no jurisdiction to review that order. See Nicholson v. Commonwealth, 300 Va. 
17, 22 (2021) (“In order to confer active jurisdiction on an appellate court, a notice of appeal must 
be timely, and it must ‘adequately identif[y] the case to be appealed.’” (alteration in original) 
(quoting Roberson v. Commonwealth, 279 Va. 396, 407 (2010))); see also Rule 5A:6. 
II. We lack a record upon which to review the trial court’s decision. 
Under Rule 5A:8(a), a transcript must be “filed in the office of the clerk of the trial court 
no later than 60 days after entry of the final judgment” to become part of the record on appeal. 
Alternatively, an appellant may submit a written statement of facts instead of a transcript under 
Rule 5A:8(c). Bay v. Commonwealth, 60 Va. App. 520, 528-29 (2012). Determining whether 
the record is sufficient to permit appellate review is a question of law that we review de novo. 
Id. at 529. 
As such, when an appellant fails to include a transcript or written statement of facts 
necessary to resolve an assignment of error, we cannot consider that assignment of error. Rule 
5A:8(b)(4)(ii); see Browning v. Browning, 68 Va. App. 19, 26-27 (2017) (“If the transcript is not 
a part of the record on appeal, we cannot consider it or any references to it in addressing [the 
appellant’s] arguments because ‘[a]n appellate court must dispose of the case upon the record 
and cannot base its decision upon appellant’s petition or brief.’” (second alteration in original) 
(quoting Smith v. Commonwealth, 16 Va. App. 630, 635 (1993))). Virginia courts have strictly 
enforced these rules. See Browning, 68 Va. App. at 31-32 (“The Rules and case law are clear: it 
is the responsibility of an appellant to provide us with a record sufficient to allow us to reach his 
or her assignments of error.”). 
However, when a transcript or written statement of facts is not indispensable to appellate 
review, we may consider the assignment of error. See Veldhuis v. Abboushi, 77 Va. App. 599, 
 - 6 - 
607 (2023) (finding “that the transcript is not indispensable to resolving this case, as we are able 
to dispose of the case by considering other portions of the record”); see also Goodpasture v. 
Goodpasture, 7 Va. App. 55, 57-58 (1988) (holding that although neither a transcript nor a 
written statement of facts was filed, the Court was able to review the assignments of error 
because the trial court’s letter opinion and order adequately stated the facts necessary to resolve 
the assignments of error). 
Here, Liberty failed to timely file either a transcript or a written statement of facts from 
the April 21, 2025 hearing concerning the alleged fraud upon what the default judgment was 
based. Unlike cases in which the trial court’s order, letter opinion, or other portions of the record 
provide sufficient facts to resolve the assignments of error, the record here does not provide an 
adequate basis for appellate review. See Veldhuis, 77 Va. App. at 607; Goodpasture, 7 Va. App. 
at 57-58. Instead, the trial court’s order states that its ruling was based on the arguments 
presented at the April 21, 2025 hearing. Because the motion and response presented multiple 
arguments, we cannot determine on which grounds the trial court based its ruling. Accordingly, 
a transcript or written statement of facts from that hearing is indispensable to resolving the 
assignments of error. Without either, however, we cannot consider those assignments of error. 
See Rule 5A:8(b)(4)(ii); Browning, 68 Va. App. at 30-31. 
CONCLUSION 
Because the October 21, 2024 order

IN THE COMMONWEALTH COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA 
 
Councilmember Jeffery Young, Jr.      : 
on behalf of and as representative      : 
of Council of the City of Philadelphia   :  
and Strawberry Mansion Community      : 
Concern          : 
   v.        :     No. 360 C.D. 2026 
           :     Argued:  October 13, 2026 
City of Philadelphia, City of       : 
Philadelphia Zoning Board of       : 
Adjustment, Philadelphia Housing      : 
Authority, Pennrose LLC,      :  
and Strawberry Mansion Housing    : 
LLC      : 
      : 
Appeal of:  Jeffery Young, Jr.      : 
 
BEFORE: HONORABLE RENÉE COHN JUBELIRER, President Judge 
 HONORABLE CHRISTINE FIZZANO CANNON, Judge (P.) 
 HONORABLE BONNIE BRIGANCE LEADBETTER, Senior Judge 
  
 
OPINION BY 
PRESIDENT JUDGE COHN JUBELIRER  FILED:  November 17, 2026   
 
 Jeffery Young, Jr. (Councilmember Young), a member of the Council of the 
City of Philadelphia (Council), appeals from the Order of the Court of Common 
Pleas of Philadelphia County (common pleas) that upheld the Decision of the City 
of Philadelphia Zoning Board of Adjustment (Board) that approved  dimensional 
variances for  an affordable housing development project located at  3230-3238 
Diamond Street  (Diamond Street Property)  being developed by the Philadelphia 
Housing Authority (Authority), Pennrose LLC, and Strawberry Mansion Housing, 
LLC (together, Pennrose) (collectively, Applicants) .  On appeal, Councilmember 
Young argues common pleas erred in finding that he waived all but one issue , and 
that the Board erred in granting the variance because Applicants did not meet their 
2 
burden of proof on multiple requirements for obtaining a variance  and Applicants 
did not hold a public meeting for the Diamond Street Property as required by Section 
14-303(12)(c)(.5) of  the Philadelphia Zoning Code (Code), 1 Title 14 of THE 
PHILADELPHIA CODE (2012) § 14-303(12)(c)(.5).  The Authority and Pennrose reply 
that the Board’s Decision should be affirmed, and Pennrose separately asserts that 
Councilmember Young lacked standing to appeal the Board’s Decision.   
 In a memorandum opinion filed July 13, 2026, this Court  held that 
Councilmember Young lacked standing based on Pennrose’s argument that there 
was no evidence that Council  Resolution 250623 (Resolution), upon which 
Councilmember Young relies to assert he has standing , was ever presented to the 
mayor for approval, which Section 6 of the First Class City Government Law (First 
Class City Law), 53 P.S. § 12526, 2 requires in order for a resolution to become 
effective.  Councilmember Young, along with the City, sought reargument  
maintaining that the First Class City Law does not apply following the adoption of 
the Philadelphia Home Rule Charter 3 (Home Rule Charter)  pursuant to the First 
Class City Home Rule Act (Home Rule Act). 4  While the Authority asserted that 
reargument was not warranted , it acknowledged that there was potential  for 
confusion as to the merits of the  standing issues raised in the Reargument 
Application, which it asserted would be resolved in Councilmember Jeffery Young, 
Jr. on behalf of and as representative of Council of the City of Philadelphia v. City 
of Philadelphia  (Pa. Cmwlth., No. 688 C.D. 2026)  (Young II ), a related case 
 
1 The Code is available at https://codelibrary.amlegal.com/codes/philadelphia/latest/ 
phildadelphia_pa/0-0-286773 (last visited November 16, 2026). 
2 Act of June 25, 1919, P.L. 581. 
3 The Home Rule Charter is available at https://codelibrary.amlegal.com/codes/ 
philadelphia/latest/phildadelphia_pa/0-0-0-262986 (last visited November 16, 2026). 
4 Act of April 21, 1949, P.L. 665, as amended, 53 P.S. §§ 13101-13157. 
3 
involving the same standing issues that is awaiting decision.  The Court granted 
reargument by Order entered  August 26, 2026 , and directed that this matter be 
argued together with Young II.  
 Following argument on this matter and Young II , we conclude that 
Councilmember Young could appeal the Board’s Decisions because the First Class 
City Law is not applicable here and Council, via the Resolution,  authorized 
Councilmember Young to file the appeal on behalf of and as the representative  of 
Council, which unquestionably has standing under the Home Rule Act .  On this 
basis, we vacate our memorandum opinion and order in this matter, Councilmember 
Jeffery Young, Jr. on behalf of and as representative of Council of the City of 
Philadelphia v. City of Philadelphia (Pa. Cmwlth., No. 360 C.D. 2026, filed July 13, 
2026) (Young I).  Upon review of the merits of this appeal, we agree with common 
pleas that all but one of the issues raised on appeal by Councilmember Young were 
waived because they were not asserted before the Board, and, on the preserved issue, 
we discern no error or abuse of discretion in the Board’s Decision .  Therefore, we 
affirm common pleas’ Order upholding that decision. 
 
I. BACKGROUND 
A. Proceedings Before the Board 
 This appeal concerns the development of the Diamond Street Property as part 
of a scattered -site affordable housing development project that utilizes 14 parcels 
located throughout the Strawberry Mansion neighborhood (the Project), which 
would consist of 55 to 57 units overall.  The Philadelphia Land Bank conveyed these 
14 parcels, which are vacant lots and described as distressed, blighted, or subject to 
“short-term dumping,” to the Authority for its use and approved Applicants’ efforts 
to obtain building permits for the Project.  (Board Decision, Findings of Fact (FOF) 
4 
¶¶ 11, 13, 15, 17 -18, 30; Board Decision, Conclusion of Law (COL) ¶ 13; 
Reproduced Record (R.R.) at 85a, 115a -16a, 128a, 130a -31a, 137a, 142a, 145a, 
166a, 430a -33a, 499a.)  Thus, the Authority owns the Project, which is being 
developed by Pennrose and will  be marketed for senior housing.  (FOF ¶¶ 11, 18, 
38; COL ¶¶ 13-14; R.R. at 191a.)  One goal of the Project was to ensure affordable 
quality units in an area where affordable housing may be an issue in the future.  (FOF 
¶¶ 18, 20, 30, 47; COL ¶¶ 13 -14; R.R. at 136a, 142a, 150a, 430a -34a, 499a.)  The 
Diamond Street Property is located within the RM-1 (Residential Multi -Family) 
zoning district .  The proposed use on this property would be Multi -Family 
Household Living and will consist of 21 dwelling units.  (FOF ¶ 2.) 
 The Philadelphia Department of Licenses and Inspections (L&I) denied a 
permit for the Diamond Street Property because 3 dimensional variances were 
needed:  1 for rear yard depth (9 feet was required, 0 was proposed), 1 for maximum 
building height (38 feet allowed, 45.5 feet proposed), and  1 for bicycle parking 
spaces (7 spaces required, 0 spaces proposed).  ( Id.)  Applicants appealed L&I’s 
denial of the permit to the Board.   (Id. ¶ 4.)  Prior to the Board holding a hearing, 
Applicants submitted a revised plan for the Diamond Street Property, clarifying that 
a pilothouse and elevator tower were part of the zoning plan.  (Id. ¶ 3.) 
 Strawberry Mansion Community Concern ( SMCC) was designated the 
coordinating Registered Community Organization (RCO) for the Project.  (Id. ¶ 14.)  
On August 23, 2024, Applicants requested a continuance of the Board hearings that 
had been scheduled at that point so that all of the hearings on the 14 properties could 
be heard together, copying Councilmember Young and SMCC’s Director Bonita 
Cummings (Cummings).  (Id. ¶ 5 n.3; R.R. at 403a.) 
5 
 Applicants emailed Cummings in December 2024, requesting a meeting with 
Cummings about other properties.  (R.R. at 679a.)  Also included in that email were 
the addresses of the 14 parcels involved in the Project and a note that a hearing on 
those parcels was scheduled before the Board on March 12, 2025.  (Id.)  Applicants 
and Cummings had a phone call on January 27, 2025, and Applicants attempted to 
follow-up by email on February 4, 11, 18, and 24, 2025, in order to schedule an RCO 
meeting.  (Id. at 674a-78a.)  Applicants copied Councilmember Young’s Director of 
Development, Conlan Crosley  (Crosley), on the February 11, 18, and 24 emails.  
SMCC did not respond to any of Applicants’ efforts.  SMCC’s counsel entered his 
appearance on March 10, 2025, and asked for a continuance of the March 12 hearing, 
which the Board granted and rescheduled a consolidated hearing for April 22, 2025.  
(Id. at 404a, 414a.)  SMCC still did not schedule any community or RCO meetings 
on the Project. 
 The Board held a hearing on April 22, 2025.5  The parties presented statements 
to the Board, and the Board received letters of support for the Project from State 
Senators Sharif Street and Vincent Hughes, State Representative Keith Harris, and 
Ryan Boyer of the Philadelphia Building and Construction Trades Council.  (FOF 
¶¶ 11-12.)  Representatives from the Authority, Strawberry Mansion Community 
Development Corporation (Strawberry Mansion CDC), and members of the 
community testified in support of the Project , including about the parcels being 
vacant lots and the presence of blight found therein .  ( Id. ¶¶ 15, 17 , 45 , 46 .)  
Representatives from Applicants and the Philadelphia City Planning Commission 
 
5 The Board’s hearing encompassed separate appeals relating to the 14 parcels.  Testimony 
regarding all of the Project, including introduction of letters of support and testimony in support 
of the Project, was intermixed with testimony related to the specific appeals of the parcels.  
Testimony regarding the Diamond Street Property is found at pages 185a to 209a of the 
Reproduced Record. 
6 
(Commission) testified about the specific development plans for the Diamond Street 
Property, the requested variances,  and the funding of the Project, particularly its 
eligibility for a federal Low Income Housing Tax Credit.  (Id. ¶¶ 10, 13, 18, 30, 34-
37, 42, 47.)  Pennrose’s representative adopted counsel’s statements regarding the 
details of the Diamond Street Property part of the Project.   (Id. ¶ 38.)  Another of 
Pennrose’s representatives testified that this property would have senior housing, as 
requested by the community, and explained why there was no bike parking planned 
due to the presence of an existing large bike parking area .  ( Id.)  A representative 
from the Commission testified that the Commission had concluded that the Project 
supported its Comprehensive Plan and that the proposed variances were minor 
deviations from the Code that were consistent with the Code’s spirit and matched 
the existing character of the surrounding area.  (Id. ¶¶ 30, 47.) 
 Councilmember Young, in whose district the Project is located, testified that 
his opposition to the Diamond Street Property variances was due to the absence of a 
community meeting for that parcel.   (Id. ¶¶ 43-44.)  Crosley, the Director of 
Development for Councilmember Young, acknowledged on cross-examination that 
Councilmember Young’s office had never requested nor organized a community 
meeting for the Diamond Street Property.  (Id. ¶ 19.)  Cummings testified on behalf 
of SMCC, the registered RCO, about concerns with the Project being comprised of 
rental units, rather than allowing for home ownership, that the Diamond Street 
Property was not initially included  in the meeting that occurred in 2019, that there 
had been no meeting for this property, that there is sufficient senior housing in the 
area, and that the proposed building was higher than the buildings facing it .  ( Id. 
¶¶ 13-14, 31, 39.)  Cummings conceded that, notwithstanding Applicants contacting 
7 
her, she had not attempted to have a community meeting  and that there was 
community support for the Project.  (Id. ¶¶ 39-40.)   
 At the end of the hearing, the Board held its vote pending discussion in 
executive session and left the record open for the parties to submit additional items.  
(Id. ¶ 48.)  Applicants submitted revised plans addressing concerns raised by the

leads.text:
IN THE COMMONWEALTH COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA 

In Re: Condemnation by the : 
Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission : 
of Property Located in the Borough : 
of West Mifflin, County of Allegheny, : 
Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, : 
for the Construction of the : 
Mon-Fayette Expressway, PA Route : 
51 to I-376 Project, a Partial Take : 
(Part of Block and Lot Nos. : 
239-D-20, 239-D-25 and 239-D-30) : 
 : No. 1357 C.D. 2024 
Appeal of: IBIS Kennywood, LLC : Submitted: June 16, 2026 

BEFORE: HONORABLE ANNE E. COVEY, Judge 
 HONORABLE STACY WALLACE, Judge 
 HONORABLE STELLA M. TSAI, Judge 

OPINION NOT REPORTED 

MEMORANDUM OPINION BY 
JUDGE COVEY FILED: November 17, 2026 

 IBIS Kennywood, LLC (Kennywood) appeals from the Allegheny 
County (County) Common Pleas Court’s (trial court) September 19, 2024 order 
overruling its preliminary objections (Preliminary Objections) to the Pennsylvania 
Turnpike Commission’s (Commission) condemnation notice. Essentially, 
Kennywood presents one issue for this Court’s review: whether the trial court erred 
as a matter of law and abused its discretion by concluding that the Co mmission 
satisfied the notice requirements of Section 305(c)(9) of the Eminent Domain Code 
(Code).1 After review, this Court affirms. 

1 26 Pa.C.S. § 305(c)(9). 
 2 
 Kennywood owns land and buildings located in the County, identified 
as Lot and Block Nos. 239 -D-20, 239 -D-25, and 239 -D-30 (collectively, the 
Property). The Property is improved by a large regional shopping center which 
contains a grocery store, a gas station with a convenience store, and retail shops. 
Kennywood has used the Property for commercial and rental purposes since 
Kennywood purchased it. On March 31, 2021, the Commission filed a Declaration 
of Taking (Declaration) which purportedly seeks to take portions of the Property, on 
both a temporary and permanent basis , to construct the Mon-Fayette Expressway, 
State Route 51 to Interstate 376 (I-376). Specifically, the Declaration seeks to take: 
(1) .426 acre, as a required right-of-way; (2) 1.997 acres, as a required temporary 
construction easement; (3) .146 acre, as a required drainage easement; (4) .834 acre, 
as a required slope easement; and (5) 2.859 acres, as a required substitute right-of-
way for Duquesne Light Company (collectively, Condemned Parcel). 
 On April 30, 2021, Kennywood filed the Preliminary Objections to the 
Declaration, alleging therein that the specified plot plans (Plot Plans) did not comply 
with Section 305(c)(9) of the Code. The trial court ordered discovery and a viewing 
of the Property. Subsequently, Kennywood deposed Commission Engineer Thomas 
Lench (Lench). Kennywood attached exhibits to Lench’s deposition transcript, 
including detailed plans regarding the proposed construction, which included the 
Plot Plans. Following discovery, the trial court stated it would not hold a hearing 
and would decide the case on the briefs, transcripts, and exhibits. On October 1, 
2021, the trial court overruled the Preliminary Objections. On October 19, 2021, 
Kennywood appealed from the trial court’s order to this Court.2 

2 This Court docketed that appeal at Commonwealth Court Docket No. 1167 C.D. 2021. 
 3 
 Thereafter, by June 16, 2022 letter, William R. Crawford, P.E. 
(Crawford), Vice President of T.W. Engineering ,3 conveyed a “summary of the 
actions taken by the . . . Commission [] in response to specific engineering concerns 
raised by [Kennywood] as part of the adjudication of the Preliminary Objection [s] 
to the [c]ondemnation of [the P roperty]” (Engineering Summary). Reproduced 
Record (R.R.) at 679a. The Engineering Summary notes that the Plot Plans “were 
part of a 75% submission (design progress prints) and not contract bid documents.” 
Id. In the June 16, 2022 letter, Crawford stated: 
It was clear to the [Commission] and its Design 
Management Team that several of the engineering 
concerns indicated in [Kennywood’s expert , Gateway 
Engineers, Inc.’s (Gateway) report] and [Gateway’s 
Project Manager, Patrick T. ] Cooper’s deposition, had 
potential to impact the subject parcel based on the 
proposed roadway design contained in the 75% plans. The 
[Commission] took these concerns seriously and directed 
the Section Designer - EADS, Inc. [(EADS)] - to 
reevaluate those design elements of the project. Based on 
this reevaluation and the progression of the final design 
plans, EADS made modifications to the design elements 
identified below between the 75% plans and the 
current [f]inal [p]lans, Specifications and Estimates for 
Section 53C2 of the Southern Section of the Mon [-
]Fayette Expressway. 
R.R. at 679a-680a (emphasis added). 
 On December 29, 2022, concluding that “[t] he trial court overlooked 
that [Kennywood] may challenge the sufficiency of the Section 305 [of the Code] 
notice, which requires a plot plan where, as here, a partial taking is at issue[,]” this 
Court vacated the trial court’s order and remanded the matter to the trial court to 
determine whether the Commission’s Plot Plans complied with Section 305(c)(9) of 

3 T.W. Engineering is a subconsultant to the Commission’s contracted engineering firm, 
HDR Engineering. 
 4 
the Code, and to issue an order disposing of Kennywood’s Preliminary Objections 
(Remand Order). 
 On February 15, 2023, the trial court issued a supplemental opinion 
(Supplemental Opinion), stating therein: 
Th[e] [trial c] ourt [] held a hearing asking the [] 
Commission for a specific plan showing the outline of the 
. . . [P]roperty with those areas proposed to be taken by the 
[] Commission. The same was supplied and these plans 
are attached to this Supplemental Opinion. It is obvious 
that this plan shows clearly and unambiguously the 
area of the partial tak [ing] that the [] Commission is 
proposing. Accordingly, with this filing, the requirement 
of [Section] 305(c)(9) [of the Code] has been met. Th[e] 
[trial c]ourt has also directed the [] Commission to make a 
separate filing under Affidavit that these are the applicable 
drawings. This filing is to be filed with the [trial] court. 
Accordingly, I believe this concludes the responsibility of 
th[e] [trial c]ourt in the above matter. 
R.R. at 847a (emphasis added). 
 On March 15, 2023, Kennywood appealed to this Court from the 
Supplemental Opinion.4 Kennywood also filed a Motion to Compel Compliance 
with Remand Order , requesting that this Court direct the trial court to resolve the 
Preliminary Objections in accordance with this Court’s Remand Order. On August 
24, 2023, this Court quashed Kennywood’s appeal as premature because the trial 
court had not yet addressed Kennywood’s Preliminary Objections and , thus, no 
appealable order existed. On September 19, 2024, the trial court overrul ed the 
Preliminary Objections and referr ed the matter to a Board of Viewers for an 
assessment of damages. On October 9, 2024, Kennywood appealed to this Court.5 

4 See Pa. Cmwlth. No. 258 C.D. 2023. 
5 This Court’s review “of a decision to condemn property and of the extent of the taking is 
to determine whether the trial court’s decision evidences an abuse of discretion or an error of law.” 
In re Redevelopment Auth. of the City of Erie, 285 A.3d 986, 990 n.2 (Pa. Cmwlth. 2022). 
 5 
 Initially, 
“[t]he power of eminent domain is an inherent one 
possessed by the Commonwealth, as sovereign, which 
permits it to take private property for a public use if the 
landowner receives just compensation for the taking. ” 
Robinson T[wp.] v. Commonwealth, . . . 147 A.3d 536, 586 
(Pa. 2016). The Code “provides a complete and exclusive 
procedure and law to govern all condemnations of 
property for public purposes and the assessment of 
damages.” [Section 102 of the Code,] 26 Pa.C.S. § 102. 
[This Court has] explained that 
[p]reliminary objections in the context of eminent 
domain actions serve a different purpose than 
preliminary objections filed in other civil actions. 
In re Condemnation of .036 Acres, More or Less, 
of Land Owned by Wexford Plaza Asso c[s.], 674 
A.2d 1204 (Pa. Cmwlth. 1996). Not only are the 
[Pennsylvania] Rules of Civil Procedure [(Civil 
Rules)] not applicable to eminent domain 
proceedings, Gilyard v. Redevelopment Auth[.] of 
Phila[.], 780 A.2d 793 (Pa. Cmwlth. 2001), but 
preliminary objections filed pursuant to [ S]ection 
[3]06 of the [Code] serve a very different purpose 
than those filed under the . . . Civil [Rules] []. In 
eminent domain cases, preliminary objections are 
intended as a procedure to resolve expeditiously 
the factual and legal challenges to a declaration of 
taking before the parties proceed to determine 
damages. N[.] Penn Water Auth [.] v. A Certain 
Parcel of Land, . . . 650 A.2d 1197 (Pa. Cmwlth. 
1994). 
In re Condemnation by City of Coatesville, 898 A.2d 1186, 
1189 n.7 (Pa. Cmwlth. 2006). Under the Code 
[p]reliminary objections shall be limited to and 
shall be the exclusive method of challenging[:] 
(i) The power or right of the condemnor to 
appropriate the condemned property unless it has 
been previously adjudicated. 
(ii) The sufficiency of the security. 
 6 
(iii) The declaration of taking[.] 
(iv) Any other procedures followed by the 
condemnor. 
[Section 306(a)(3)(i)-(iv) of the Code,] 26 Pa.C.S. § 
306(a)(3)(i)-(iv). 
In re Condemnation of Premises Owned by Powell, 260 A.3d 298, 307 -08 (Pa. 
Cmwlth. 2021). 
The . . . Code sets forth the requirements of notice that 
must be given by a condemnor. It states in relevant part as 
follows: 
(c) Contents. --The notice to be given the 
condemnee shall state: 
. . . . 
(8) A statement that the condemnee’s property has 
been condemned and a reasonable identification of 
the property. 
(9) In the case of a partial taking , a plot plan 
showing the condemnee’s entire property and 
the area taken. 
(10) A statement of the nature of the title acquired. 
(11) A statement specifying where a plan showing 
the condemned property may be inspected in the 
county in which the property taken is located. 
. . . . 
[Section 305(c)(8)-(11) of the Code,] 26 Pa.C.S. § 
305(c)(8)-(11). 
Burns v. Dep’t of Transp., 364 A.3d 461, 466-67 (Pa. Cmwlth. 2025) (italic emphasis 
omitted; bold emphasis added). 
The importance of an accurate plot plan has been 
explained by this Court as follows: 
 7 
The plot plans and property plat filed with the 
declaration of taking and served upon a 
condemnee are part of and indeed, the heart of a 
declaration of taking . It is only by reference to 
such plans that one can determine what property is 
the subject of condemnation and, in the case of a 
partial taking, what part of a property has been 
taken. 
W[.] Whiteland Assoc[s.] v. [Dep’t of Transp.], 690 A.2d 
1266, 1269 (Pa. Cmwlth. 1997) (emphasis added). [The 
Pennsylvania] Supreme Court [(Supreme Court)] has held 
that where a plot plan does not “establish the extent or 
effect of the taking[,]” the condemnee is not bound by the 
30-day deadline in Section 306(a) of the . . . Code for filing 
preliminary objections to a declaration of taking. Szabo v. 
Commonwealth, . . . 202 A.3d 52, 53 (Pa. 2019) (Opinion 
Announcing the Judgment of the Court) . . . . 
Burns, 364 A.3d at 468 (bold emphasis added).6 

 6 In Burns, a condemnee appealed from the trial court’s order striking an allegation in the 
condemnee’s petition requesting appointment of viewers, which asserted that the Pennsylvania 
Department of Transportation’s ( PennDOT) declaration of taking did not include an accurate

effected the de facto condemnation of her property. PennDOT’s plot plan depicted the condemned 
area of the condemnee’s property and included the rectangular outline of the condemnee’s

right-of-way. The condemnee obtained her own survey and thereby learned that the expanded

leads.court: New Jersey Superior Court Appellate Division
leads.text:
SUPERIOR COURT OF NEW JERSEY 
 APPELLATE DIVISION 
 DOCKET NO . A-3106-24 

THE BANK OF NEW YORK 
MELLON f/k/a THE BANK OF 
NEW YORK AS TRUSTEE FOR 
THE CERTIFICATEHOLDERS 
OF CWALT, INC., ALTERNATIVE 
LOAN TRUST 2005-6CB, 
MORTGAGE PASS THROUGH 
CERTIFICATES, SERIES 2005 -6CB, 

 Plaintiff -Respondent, 

v. 

WAYNE LEE MARTIN, 

 Defendant -Appellant, 

and 

RONA LYNN HOLMES -MARTIN, 
STATE OF NEW JERSEY , and 
STATE FARM NORTH, 

 Defendants. 
_______________________________ 

Submitted October 15, 2026 – Decided November 17, 2026 

Before Judges De Almeida and Augostini. 
NOT FOR PUBLICATION WITHOUT THE 
APPROVAL OF THE APPELLATE DIVISION 

This opinion shall not "constitute precedent or be binding upon any court ." Although it is posted on the 
internet , this opinion is binding only on the parties in the case and its use in other cases is limited . R. 1:36 -3. 

2 A-3106 -24 

On appeal from the Superior Court of New Jersey, 
Chancery D ivision, Essex County, Docket No. 
F-000361 -24. 

Wayne Lee Martin, self -represented appellant. 

Matthew M. Siti (Leopold & Associates, PLLC ), 
attorney for respondent . 

PER CURIAM 

 In this residential foreclosure action , d efendant Wayne Lee Martin 
(Martin) appeals from two orders: an August 16, 2024 order granting summary 
judgment to plaintiff The Bank of New York Mellon F/K/A The Bank of New 
York as Trustee for the Certificate Holders of CWALT, Inc., Alternative Loan 
Trust 2005-6CB, Mortgage Pass Through Certificates, Series 2005 -6CB; and a 
May 6, 2025 final judgment . We affirm . 
I. 
On January 3, 2005, Martin and Rona Lynn Holmes -Martin (collectively 
defendant s) borrowed $184,000 from Gateway Funding Diversified Mortgage 
Services L.P., D /B/A Ivy Mortgage (Gateway). Martin executed and delivered 
a note to Gateway promising to repay the loan (Note). Defendants executed a 
mortgage to secure the loan, and the mortgage was given to Mortgage Electronic 
Registration Systems, Inc. (MERS) as nominee for Gateway. 

3 A-3106 -24 

In 2008, MERS assigned the Note and mortgage to The Bank of New York 
as Trustee for the Certificate Holders of CWALT 2005 -06CB (The Bank of New 
York). In 2022, defendants executed a loan modification agreement to NewRez 
LLC D/B/A Shellpoint Mortgage Servicing as Attorney in Fact for plaintiff. In 
2023, The Bank of New York assigned the Note and mortgage to plaintiff. Both 
assignments were recorded. 
 In July 2023 , defendants ceased paying the amounts due under the Note 
and mortgage and have not made any payments since then. O n November 30, 
2023, plaintiff sent defendants a notice of default and intent to foreclose . On 
January 11, 2024 , plaintiff filed a foreclosure complaint against defendants . On 
January 30, 2024, Martin filed an answer , in which he denied the complaint 's 
allegations regarding default but admitted "ma[king] payments up to July 2023 
[but] none thereafter. " Martin acknowledged "having possession of and rights 
to [the] subject property " but denied plaintiff 's right to enforce the Note and 
mortgage. 
 After a trial date was scheduled, plaintiff moved for summary judgment. 
In support of the motion, plaintiff submitted a certification from Anna Milan , 
document verification specialist for plaintiff 's servicer . Milan certified she 
personally reviewed plaintiff 's business records pertaining to this matter , finding 

4 A-3106 -24 

"[p]laintiff has physical possession of the Note and is the holder of the Note and 
[m]ortgage, " thereby giving it standing to foreclose . Regarding the mortgage, 
Milan certified it had been assigned to MERS as nominee for Gateway in 2005; 
to The Bank of New York in 2008 ; and to plaintiff in 2023 . Also, defendants 
executed a loan modification agreement with the servicer of the Note and 
mortgage in 2022 . Milan attached to her certification the Note, endorsements, 
mortgage, assignments , modification agreement , and notice of intention to 
foreclose. Defendants did not oppose the motion. 
On August 16, 2024 , the Chancery Division granted summary judgment 
to plaintiff with an accompanying statement of reasons . A final judgment of 
foreclosure was entered on May 6, 202 5. The judgment awarded plaintiff 
$342,154.76, plus costs, fees, and post-judgment interest , and allowed plaintiff 
to sell the mortgaged property to satisfy some o f the amount owed. 
II. 
 On appeal, Martin raises only one argument for our consideration . He 
claims the Chancery Division erred by relying on an u nrelated statement of 
material facts in support of plaintiff 's motion. 
We review a summary judgment ruling de novo, applying the same 
standard used by the trial courts. Samolyk v. Berthe , 251 N.J. 73 , 78 (2022) 

5 A-3106 -24 

(citing Woytas v. Greenwood Tree Experts, Inc. , 237 N.J. 501, 511 (2019)) . 
"The court 's function is not 'to weigh the evidence and determine the truth of the 
matter but to determine whether there is a genuine issue for trial. '" Rios v. Meda 
Pharm., Inc. , 247 N.J. 1, 13 (2021) (quoting Brill v. Guardian Life Ins. Co. of 
Am., 142 N.J. 520, 540 (1995) ). But we review a decision granting final 
judgment of foreclosure for abuse of discretion. Customers Bank v. Reitnour 
Inv. Prop s., LP , 453 N.J. Super 338, 348 (App. Div. 2018) (citing Sears Mortg . 
Corp. v. Rose , 134 N.J. 326, 354 (1993)) . 
 Martin correctly point s out that plaintiff submitted a n unrelated statement 
of material fact s in support of its summary judgment motion . The statement 
referred to an unrelated defendant and property located in another county . 
Martin, however, does not refute the facts certified by Milan , nor does he raise 
any substantive challenge to the court 's summary judgment findings. 
Pursuant to Rule 4:46-2(a), a party moving for summary judgment must 
file a "statement of each material fact as to which the movant contends there is 
no genuine issue together with a citation to the portion of the motion record 
establishing the fact or demonstrating that it is uncontroverted. " Rule 4:46-2(b) 
mandates "[a] party opposing the motion shall file a responding statement either 
admitting or disputing each of the facts in the movant 's statement. " "[A]ll 

6 A-3106 -24 

material facts in the movant 's statement which are sufficiently supported will be 
deemed admitted . . . unless specifically disputed by citation [to the portion of 
the motion record] demonstrating the existence of a genuine issue as to the fact. " 
Ibid. 
Rule 4:46-5(a) provides "an adverse party may not rest upon the mere 
allegations [in] the pleading[s], but must respond by affidavits meeting the 
requirements of [Rule] 1:6 -6 . . . setting forth specific facts showing that there 
is a genuine issue for trial. " Rule 1:6-6 states affi davits must be "made on 
personal knowledge , setting forth only facts which are admissible in evidence 
to which the affiant is competent to testify. " 
In this case, Martin failed to file a response to plaintiff 's statement of 
material facts or oppose the motion for summary judgment . Accordingly, the 
court reviewed the Milan certification and attachments, properly determined 
from those documents the uncontested facts, and deemed those facts admitted. 
The court did not rely on the incorrect statement of material facts . Based on our 
de novo review, we are convinced the court correctly granted summary judgment 
to plaintiff. 
We add only the following admonition. The seriousness of a foreclosure 
action cannot be understated. Pleadings by whi ch court action is sought require 

7 A-3106 -24 

skill, care, and attention . The carelessness in the filings in this case may have 
been excusable due to an honest mistake , see Mancini v. E ds ex rel. New Jersey 
Automobile Full Insurance Underwriting Association , 132 N.J. 330, 335 (1993) . 
However , plaintiff must exercise greater diligence going forward . 
Affirmed.

IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF THE STATE OF WASHINGTON 

HOUSING AUTHORITY OF THE CITY 
OF SEATTLE, a Washington public 
body corporate and politic, 

 Appellant, 

 v. 

JOAN HUYNH, HUNG TRAN, and 
JONATHAN TRAN, et al., 

 Respondents. 

 No. 88425-5-I 

 DIVISION ONE 

ORDER GRANTING 
MOTION TO PUBLISH 

Appellant filed a motion to publish on September 14, 2026. A panel of the 
court called for an answer which respondent filed on October 23. After 
consideration of the motion and answer the panel has determined that the motion 
to publish shall be granted. 
Now, therefore, it is hereby 
ORDERED that the motion to publish is granted. 
FOR THE COURT: 

IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF THE STATE OF WASHINGTON 

HOUSING AUTHORITY OF THE CITY 
OF SEATTLE, a Washington public 
body corporate and politic, 

 Appellant, 

 v. 

JOAN HUYNH, HUNG TRAN, and 
JONATHAN TRAN, et al., 

 Respondent. 

 No. 88425-5-I 

 DIVISION ONE 

 UNPUBLISHED OPINION 

 H
AZELRIGG, C.J. — The Housing Authority of the City of Seattle appeals 
from the dismissal of its unlawful detainer action against tenants in default as to 
rent, based on the trial court’s interpretation of RCW 59.18.190. Because the trial 
court erred in its interpretation of the statute, we reverse, vacate the order of limited 
dissemination, and remand. 

FACTS 
On September 16, 2024, the Housing Authority of the City of Seattle (SHA), 
in its capacity as a landlord, issued a notice to Joan Huynh, Hung Tran, and 
Jonathan Tran (collectively, Huynh) to pay their past due rent or vacate the 
apartment where they resided. The notice stated that Huynh was “ not in 
compliance with the terms of the lease agreement ” because they owed $6,686 in 
rent payments from the preceding nine consecutive months and nonpayment of 

No. 88425-5-I/2 
- 2 - 
the rent owed within 30 days of the notice would result in the termination of the 
lease on October 17. On November 7, Huynh was still in possession of the 
apartment, and SHA personally served them with a summons and complaint for 
unlawful detainer. Among other relief requested in the complaint, SHA sought 
damages in the amount of the unpaid rent and a writ of restitution to restore its 
possession of the apartment. SHA did not file the complaint in the superior court 
until February 20, 2025. On February 28, a commissioner issued an order to show 
cause and set a hearing for April 2. On March 6, SHA filed a declaration of service 
signed by a SHA paralegal who declared that she served three copies of the show 
cause order on the tenants via regular mail. 
Huynh appeared remotely at the April 2 hearing and was present when the 
trial court certified the case for assignment to a judge and set a subsequent hearing 
on April 30. The following day, the chief civil judge assigned the case to a judge, 
struck the April 30 hearing, and set a trial date in June. On April 11, the assigned 
judge struck the June trial and reset the show cause hearing for April 21. On April 
14, the same SHA paralegal who had done so previously filed another declaration 
of service indicating that she had served three copies of the order setting the April 
21 show cause hearing by regular mail. 
Huynh was not present at the April 21 show cause hearing, and the trial 
court ultimately entered findings of fact and conclusions of law and judgment in the 
case. The judge found that Huynh had been properly served the notice to pay or 
vacate on September 16, 2024, “materially breached the lease by failing to pay 
rent when due and failing to pay the amount alleged before the expiration of time 
No. 88425-5-I/3 
- 3 - 
in the statutory notice to [p]ay or [v]acate,” “failed to cure the breach within the time 
specified in the statutory notice, ” and continued both to “ be in arrears in rent . . . 
and . . . in possession of the unit.” The court concluded that this material breach 
entitled SHA to both damages and immediate possession of the premises and 
entered a judgment and a writ of restitution to that effect. 
 Three days later, Huynh filed a handwritten pro se motion to vacate the 
judgment and stay enforcement of the judgment and the writ. Therein, Huynh 
explained that she did not understand that the court date had been moved to April 
21 and thought that the scheduling order she received was for a settlement 
meeting. She further asserted that she did not recall receiving scheduling 
information about the hearings, requested a Vietnamese interpreter, and attached 
an image of a check to SHA as proof of partial payment of the delinquent rent. 
SHA opposed Huynh’ s motion to vacate; it argued that Huynh had failed to pay 
rent for over a year, despite its attempts to provide opportunities for repayment, 
and otherwise failed to show grounds to justify vacatur of the judgment. 
Specifically, it argued the relevant standards under CR 60 regarding motions to 
vacate, that the judgment was not obtained by irregular means or void due to a 
lack of jurisdiction, and Huynh had not shown excusable neglect in their failure to 
timely contest entry of the judgment. 
 The trial court granted Huynh’ s motion to vacate on May 2 and set a new 
show cause hearing for later that month. On May 9, Huynh, now represented by 
counsel, disclosed their defenses as ordered by the trial court , including the one 
relevant to this appeal: that SHA had “failed to comply with RCW 59.18.190, as [it] 
No. 88425-5-I/4 
- 4 - 
failed to seek a remedy within 60 days of purportedly serving the predicate notice 
on” Huynh. 
On May 16, the trial court held the show cause hearing. Huynh again 
argued procedural defenses and emphasized that SHA had failed to comply with 
RCW 59.18.190, a key provision of the R esidential Landlord-Tenant Act of 19731 
(RLTA), because service of a summons and complaint “ are not contemplated as 
pursuing a remedy. ” SHA disagreed and asserted that RCW 59.18.190 did not 
“provide specific guidelines for filing and service, ” SHA was simply required “ to 
seek a remedy,” and it had done so by effectuating service of process on Huynh. 
Due to time constraints, t he trial court continued the hearing and allowed both 
parties to submit additional briefing prior to the next court date. On May 27, the 
trial court took up the remaining issues , heard from the parties, and entered its 
written order. 
In its order on SHA ’s motion to show cause, the trial court “ agree[d] that 
service of a summons and a complaint may commence an action” but concluded 
that this did not constitute the pursuit of a remedy for purposes of the RLTA. It 
further noted a remedy cannot be “awarded without first filing a complaint ” and 
“RCW 59.18 [sic] must be strictly construed in favor of the tenant. ” It reasoned 
that because SHA had “ not pursue[d] a remedy within the 60 -day timeline 
pr[e]scribed by RCW 59.18.190, the predicate eviction notice expired” and the 
court lacked authority to grant SHA relief. The trial court dismissed the unlawful 

1 Ch. 59.18 RCW. 
No. 88425-5-I/5 
- 5 - 
detainer action without prejudice, agreed that an order of limited dissemination was 
warranted, and struck the trial dates that had been set. 
SHA timely appealed. 

ANALYSIS 
I. Interpretation of RCW 59.18.190 
SHA’s sole contention on appeal is that the trial court erred in its 
interpretation of RCW 59.18.190 because “commencing an unlawful detainer 
action is the first step in obtaining a judicial order to evict a tenant who remains in 
possession of the property. ” It avers that “ pursuing a remedy ,” as used in the 
statute, “clearly means electing and initiating a process through which the landlord 
can begin to enforce its rights and obtain legal relief provided by the statute through 
the judicial process.” Huynh responds that there are no remedies “available to a 
landlord that has not both served the tenant with process and filed the case with 
the court ” and “service of process alone is not sufficient to pursue a remedy 
because it does not place the controversy within the power of the court to 
adjudicate.” SHA is correct. 
“The meaning of a statute is a question of law reviewed de novo.” Dep’t of 
Ecology v. Campbell & Gwinn, LLC , 146 Wn.2d 1, 9, 43 P.3d 4 (2002). The 
reviewing “court’s fundamental objective is to ascertain and carry out the 
Legislature’s intent, and if the statute’s meaning is plain on its face, then the court 
must give effect to that plain meaning as an expression of legislative intent.” Id. at 
9-10. “Plain meaning is discerned from the ordinary meaning of the language at 
issue, the context of the statute in which that provision is found, related provisions, 
No. 88425-5-I/6 
- 6 - 
and the statutory scheme as a whole.” Christensen v. Ellsworth, 162 Wn.2d 365, 
373, 173 P.3d 228 (2007). “We must assign familiar legal terms in a statute their 
familiar legal meaning.” Floeting v. Grp. Health Co- op., 200 Wn. App. 758, 764, 
403 P.3d 559 (2017) , aff’d, 192 Wn.2d 848, 434 P.3d 39 (2019) . “ Statutory 
provisions and rules should be harmonized whenever possible.” Christensen, 162 
Wn.2d at 373. We consider “‘the broader statutory context for guidance,’” but “‘we 
must not add words where the legislature has chosen not to include them, and we 
must construe statutes such that all of the language is given effect. ’” Randy 
Reynolds & Assocs., Inc. v. Harmon, 193 Wn.2d 143, 155-56, 437 P.3d 677 (2019) 
(internal quotation marks omitted) (quoting Lake v. Woodcreek Homeowners 
Ass’n, 169 Wn.2d 516, 526, 243 P.3d 1283 (2010)). “ [I]f, after this inquiry, the 
statute remains susceptible to more than one reasonable meaning, the statute is 
ambiguous and it is appropriate to resort to aids to construction, including 
legislative history.” Campbell & Gwinn, 146 Wn.2d at 12. 
 The RLTA requires tenants to “pay the rental amount at such times and in 
such amounts as provided for in the rental agreement. ” RCW 59.18.130. If the 
landlord learns that a tenant is in breach of this obligation, they “ may immediately 
give notice to the tenant to remedy the nonconformance. Said notice shall expire 
after sixty days unless the landlord pursues any remedy under this chapter.” RCW 
59.18.190 (emphasis added). 
“The unlawful detainer statute is in derogation of the common law, and must 
therefore be strictly construed in favor of the tenant.” Hous. Auth. of City of Everett 
v. Terry, 114 Wn.2d 558, 563, 789 P.2d 745 (1990). The unlawful detainer cause 
No. 88425-5-I/7 
- 7 - 
of action is “‘designed to hasten the recovery of possession’” by the landlord but, 
“in order to take advantage of its favorable provisions, a landlord must comply with 
the requirements of the statute. ” Id. at 563 -64 (quoting Wilson v. Daniels , 31 
Wn.2d 633, 643- 44, 198 P.2d 496 (1948)). Tenants can be liable for unlawful 
detainer for a variety of reasons, including when they remain in possession of the 
residence “after a default in the payment of rent, and after notice in writing requiring 
in the alternative the payment of the rent or the surrender of the detained 
premises.” RCW 59.12.030(3). “Once a tenant is in the status of unlawful detainer, 
the landlord may commence an unlawful detainer action by serving a summons 
and complaint.” Indigo Real Est . Servs., Inc. v. Wadsworth , 169 Wn. App. 412, 
421, 280 P.3d 506 (2012) (emphasis added); RCW 59.12.070. 
 To determine the plain meaning of the phrase “pursues any remedy,” as 
used in RCW 59.18.190, we consider the “ordinary meaning of the language at 
issue, the context of the statute in which that provision is found, related provisions, 
and the statutory scheme as a whole. ” Christensen, 162 Wn.2d at 373 . While 
“remedy” is not explicitly defined, the phrase “remedy under this chapter,” as well 
as similar variations, is used throughout the statutory scheme. See , e.g., RCW 
59.18.020;
2 .090;3 .160.4 We have previously held that remedies available under 
the RLTA include “recovery of related possession, related
